Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 74, verse 1–2:

[Page 294]
﴿O you who are wrapped up,﴾ ﴿arise and warn!﴾ The Prophet (ﷺ) was addressed by this attribute in a particular state he was in at the time the surah was revealed, namely that when he saw the angel between heaven and earth, he was frightened by seeing him, so he returned to Khadijah and said: "Wrap me up, wrap me up," or he said, "Cover me," or he said, "Cover me, then wrap me up," according to the differing narrations, and the reconciling of them is evident. So she wrapped him up, and then ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ was revealed.

It has already passed, at the words of His Exalted saying ﴿O you who are wrapped in garments﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 1], what this address contains of honour and gentleness.

Al-Muddaththir: an active participle from tadaththara, meaning he put on the difar (dithar, cloak). Its original form is al-mutadaththir, and the ta' was assimilated into the dal because the two are close in pronunciation, as occurred in the verb (idda'a) (to claim).

Al-dithar, with a kasra on the dal: the garment worn over the garment that is worn directly on the body, which is called al-shi'ar (the undergarment). In a hadith: "The Ansar are the shi'ar (undergarment), and the people are the dithar (outer garment)."

So the description "al-Muddaththir" is literal. It has been said that it is metaphorical, meaning "one wrapped in prophethood," just as one says "he wore the mantle of glory and girded himself with it," in the manner that was said regarding His Exalted saying ﴿O you who are wrapped in garments﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 1], i.e., O you who wear the robe of prophethood and its cloak.

The standing commanded is not used in its literal sense, because the Prophet (ﷺ), when this was revealed to him, was neither sleeping nor lying down, nor was he commanded to rise on his feet. Rather, it is used metaphorically or allusively to mean hastening, turning toward, and resolving upon warning.

This usage of the verb "standing" became so widespread that the meaning of beginning an action became one of the meanings of the root qiyam, equal to the literal sense, and it came with this meaning in much of their speech. Ibn Malik, in al-Tashil, counted the verb qama (to stand) among the verbs of beginning. The use of the verb of standing in the sense of beginning may be an allusion to what necessarily accompanies standing, namely resolve and determination, as in the verse. In al-Kashshaf he said: "Arise with the standing of resolve and determination."

The explicit meaning may also be intended alongside the allusive meaning, such as the words of Murrah ibn Mahkan al-Tamimi, one of the poets of al-Hamasah:

[Page 295]
O mistress of the house, rise, not humbled, gather to yourself the men of the tribe and the strangers.

When the verb of standing, in this usage, is joined to a verb, the combination yields the meaning of beginning the action earnestly. They cited the words of Hassan ibn al-Mundhir:

Since he has risen to revile me, a base man, like a pig rolling in ashes.

And the words of a poet, which is among the evidences of grammar, whose speaker is unknown:

So he rose, defending the people from her with his sword, and said: "Alas, there is no way to Hind."

The fa' in (fa-andhir) indicated that the warning follows directly upon the readiness and beginning in the command. So the verb (qum) is treated as intransitive, and the consequence (fa-andhir) following it clarifies the intended meaning of the command to stand.

The meaning: O you who are wrapped up in fear at seeing the angel of revelation, do not be afraid, and turn to warning.

It appears that this verse is the first revealed concerning the command to call to the message, because the surah al-Alaq did not contain a command to call. The opening of surah al-Muzzammil implies that he had already been preceded by the call, given His saying in it ﴿Indeed, We have sent to you a messenger as a witness over you﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 15], and His saying ﴿And leave Me with the deniers﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 11]. Their denial came only after he had informed them that he was a messenger of God to them, and the command to warn began; because warning encompasses the meanings of cautioning against doing what is unbecoming and its consequences, so warning deserves to precede the command to praiseworthy deeds, for clearing away is prior to adorning, and averting harms takes precedence over securing benefits. And because most of the conditions of people at that time needed warning and caution.

The object of (andhir) is omitted to indicate generality, meaning: warn all people, and they were at that time all people except Khadijah, may Allah be pleased with her, for she had believed, so she was deserving of good tidings.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 74, verse 3:

﴿And your Lord, glorify﴾. "Your Lord" (rabbaka) is in the accusative as the object of the verb "glorify" (kabbir), placed before its governing verb to indicate exclusivity (ikhtisas). That is: do not glorify anyone other than Him. This is a restriction of singling out (qasr ifrad), meaning: rather than the idols.

صفحة ٢٩٦

The conjunction "and" (waw) connects the clause "And your Lord, glorify" to the clause "Arise and warn" [al-Muddaththir: 2].

The particle "fa" (then) entered upon "glorify" to signal an omitted conditional clause of which "glorify" is the response. This is a general condition, since there is no evidence for a specific one, and the placement of the object before the verb prepares for the supposition of the condition. For the fronting of a complement may be treated as the equivalent of a condition, as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "So in both of them, strive" (fa-fihima fa-jahid), meaning the two parents.

So the implied meaning is: "Whatever may be the case, then glorify your Lord."

The meaning is that he should not cease from proclaiming the glorification of God and His unity at every time and in every state. This is a form of concision (ijaz). Ibn Jinni permitted that the "fa" be superfluous, saying: it is like your saying "Zayd, then strike," meaning: "Zayd, strike."

The glorification (takbir) of the Lord is His exaltation. The verb "kabbir" conveys the sense of attributing to its object the origin of its root derivation, and this is one of the meanings of the form "fa'{{ʿ}}ala" (faʿʿala): that is, inform about Him with a report of exaltation. This is a figurative glorification, by likening the thing being exalted to a great thing of its kind, on the common ground of its excellence over others in the attributes of its kind.

Thus the meaning of "And your Lord, glorify": describe your Lord with attributes of exaltation. This includes declaring Him free from deficiencies, which encompasses affirming His divinity and His being free from offspring, and it includes describing Him with all attributes of perfection.

The meaning of "glorify" (kabbir): glorify Him in your belief, and glorify Him in your speech by praising and proclaiming Him. This meaning includes that one says "Allahu Akbar" (God is greatest), since when one says this phrase it conveys that God is described as greater than every great thing, that is, more exalted and more transcendent than every majestic thing. For this reason this phrase was made the opening of the prayer (salah).

I reckon that in the mention of takbir there is an allusion to the legislation of the prayer, whose beginning is the takbir, especially its being joined with His saying "And your garments, purify" [al-Muddaththir: 4], for this is an allusion to the legislation of purity. Perhaps this is a preparation for the legislation of the prayer. In the narration of Ma'mar from al-Zuhri in Muslim it occurred that he said: "And that was before the prayer was prescribed." The apparent view is that God made the prayer obligatory upon him following this surah, and it was other than the five daily prayers, for it is established that he prayed in al-Masjid al-Haram.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 74, verse 4:

Page 297
﴿And your garments, purify﴾ — in its arrangement (naẓm) it is like the arrangement of ﴿and your Lord, glorify﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 3], meaning: do not neglect purifying your garments.

Garments (thiyab) have a plain, literal usage, which is what a wearer puts on, and a metonymic usage, in which "garments" stands for the person of their owner, as in the verse of ʿAntarah:

"So I pierced with the stout spear his garments"
This is a metonym (kināyah) for thrusting him with the spear.

Purification (taṭhīr) has a literal usage, which is cleaning and removing impurities (najāsāt), and a figurative usage, which is purification in the sense of moral purification (tazkiyah). God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah intends only to remove from you the impurity, O people of the household, and to purify you with complete purification﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 33].

Both meanings are suitable in the verse, so both are taken together, which yields four meanings. He is commanded with the true purity of his garments, to nullify what the people of the Jahiliyyah were upon of disregard for this matter. Hadiths have been reported on this, some of which strengthen others, and the strongest of them is what al-Tirmidhi narrated: "Indeed Allah is clean and loves cleanliness," and he said: it is gharīb.

The purification of his body is more fitting (by priority).

The connection of purification with this meaning is that it is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to ﴿and your Lord, glorify﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 3], because when he was commanded with prayer, he was commanded with purifying himself for it, since purity is prescribed for prayer.

The Qur'an mentions purity of garments only in this verse, in one of its possible interpretations, and he is commanded to purify himself.

The meaning composed of the metonymic and the figurative is the most fitting, given the attribution of prophethood to him. In the speech of the Arabs: so-and-so is clean of garments (naqiyy al-thiyab). Ghaylan ibn Salamah al-Thaqafi said:

"And by the praise of God, I have not worn the garment of a wicked one, nor do I veil myself with treachery"

They also recited the verse of Abu Kabshah, which is attributed to Imru' al-Qays:

"The garments of ʿAwf are pure and clean, and their faces are white at the travelers' gatherings, bright"

Page 298
The entry of the fāʾ (fa) upon the verb (fa-ṭahhir) is as previously explained at the words ﴿and your Lord, glorify﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 3].

The fronting of (thiyabaka) before the verb (ṭahhir) is for emphasis on it in the command to purify.

﴿And uncleanness, forsake﴾. *Al-rijz*: it is said with a kasra on the rā’ (*ri*jz) and with a ḍamma (*ru*jz), and these are two dialects for it, and the meaning is one according to the majority of the people of the language. Abū al-ʿĀliyah, al-Rabīʿ and al-Kisāʾī said: *al-rijz*, with a kasra, means punishment, impurity and disobedience, and with a ḍamma it means idol. Here *al-rijz* is taken to include idols and other things, such as eating carrion and blood.

The placing of *al-rijz* before the verb *uhjur* (forsake) is for emphasis, since the command to abandon it is the general concern here.

The discussion of ﴿*wa al-rujza fa-uhjur*﴾ is like the discussion of ﴿*wa rabbaka fakabbir*﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 3].

*Al-hajr* means cutting off association and not coming close to a thing. Here *al-hajr* is a metaphor for abandoning any involvement with the specific conditions of each kind of *rijz*, each in the manner that suits it according to people's custom.

The command to forsake *rijz* necessarily entails that one does not worship idols and that one denies divinity to them.

﴿And do not confer favour, expecting to receive more.﴾ The connection of ﴿and do not confer favour, expecting to receive more﴾ to the command to abandon *al-rujz* (idolatry) is that conferring favour in giving is much a trait of the people of polytheism. When God commanded him to abandon *al-rujz*, He forbade him from the traits of the people of *al-rujz*, with a prohibition that implies, by way of *kinaya* (allusion), the command to give charity and to give it abundantly. It is as if He had said: "Give charity, and give abundantly in charity, and do not confer favour," meaning: do not regard what you have given as much, so that you hold back from giving more, or so that regret about what you have given creeps into you.

The *sin* and *ta'* in His saying (*tasta'thiru*, "you regard as much") denote counting, meaning: after you have given much.

This is one of the fine forms of emphasis on the commanded act being accomplished: charity is treated as though it had already occurred, because it is among the traits of the Prophet (ﷺ), since he was the most generous of people, and this was known of him even before his prophethood. God had prepared him for noble character. Khadija said to him in the hadith of the beginning of revelation: "Indeed, you carry the burdens of others, you earn what is lost, you ..." Thus this verse contains an allusion to giving charity, just as it contains an allusion to prayer, and it is a habit of the Qur'an to combine prayer and *zakat* (obligatory almsgiving).

*Al-mann* (conferring favour): reminding the benefactor's beneficiary of his benefaction.

*Al-istikthar*: regarding a thing as abundant, meaning: do not magnify what you give.

This prohibition conveys the generality of every act of regarding as much, whatever amount one gives. The earliest exegetes gave interpretations of its meaning, ﴿and do not confer favour, expecting to receive more﴾, none of which is suitable to the connection; al-Qurtubi counted them up to eleven.

﴿Tasta'thiru﴾ is a clause in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) from the pronoun in ﴿tamunnu﴾, and it is a *hal muqaddara* (a qualifier anticipated in meaning, i.e. the act is to be understood as not yet done in that respect).

[p. 299]

**﴿And for your Lord, be patient﴾**: an affirmation (*tathbit*) for the Prophet (ﷺ) to endure what he meets of the harm of the polytheists and the hardships of the call.

**Sabr** (patience): the steadfastness of the soul and its bearing of hardships, pains and the like.

The verbal noun *sabr* and the words derived from it carry the sense of enduring something arduous.

The verb *sabara* takes the object of what the patient one endures with the particle **ʿalā** ("upon"), as in *ṣabara ʿalā al-adhā* (he was patient under the harm). It also carries the sense of submitting to something arduous, and in that case it takes the object of what is endured with the particle **li-** ("for"). The context favours one of the two constructions, so one does not say *iṣbir ʿalā Allāh* ("be patient upon God"), but one says *iṣbir ʿalā ḥukm Allāh* or *li-ḥukm Allāh* ("be patient under God's judgement" or "for God's judgement"). Thus the **lām** in **li-rabbika** may be the lām that transitively governs the verb *sabr*, with an elided noun understood: *iṣbir li-amrihi wa-takālīf waḥyihi* ("be patient for His command and the obligations of His revelation"), as He said: ﴿And be patient for the judgement of your Lord, for you are before Our eyes﴾ [al-Tur: 48] in Surat al-Tur, and His saying: ﴿And be patient for the judgement of your Lord, and do not obey from among them a sinner or a disbeliever﴾ [al-Insan: 24] in Surat al-Insan. This suits His address with **﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾** [al-Muddaththir: 1], because he wrapped himself out of the intensity of the impact of seeing the angel. The omission of the mention of the noun governed by the preposition allows the soul to go to everything that belongs to the concerns of the one addressed in relation to him.

Page 300

It is also possible that the **lām** is the lām of causation (*lām al-taʿlīl*, "for the sake of"), and the object of the verb *sabr* is omitted, meaning: be patient for the sake of your Lord in respect of everything that is hard for you.

The placing of **li-rabbika** before **iṣbir** serves to emphasise the matters for the sake of which he is patient, while also observing the rhyme (*al-fāṣila*, the verse-ending rhyme). Some scholars took the **lām** in **li-rabbika** to be the lām of causation, meaning: be patient in respect of their harm for His sake. This would mean that he is patient trusting (*tawakkul*) that God will take on their recompense. This interpretation rests on the premise that the occasion of the revelation of the surah was what befell the Prophet (ﷺ) of the harm of the polytheists.

Patience (*sabr*) was discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 45] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Expressing God by the description **"your Lord"** indicates that this patience is an act of piety towards the Master and obedience to Him.

These, then, are six counsels which God enjoined upon His Messenger (ﷺ) at the outset of his mission, and they are among the comprehensive sayings of the Qur'an. God intended by them to purify His Messenger and to make him an exemplar for his community.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 74, verses 8–10:

﴿So when the trumpet is sounded﴾ ﴿that will be, that Day, a difficult Day﴾ ﴿for the disbelievers, not easy.﴾

The fa' (فَ, "so/then") indicates that this warning is a consequence of the command to warn in His saying "fa-andhir" (so warn), meaning: warn those who are warned, and warn them at the time of the nuqr (نَقْرَ) in the naqur (النَّاقُور), and what will befall on that Day those who were warned yet turned away from the reminder. For the fa' must be connected to the speech that precedes it.

It is also possible that it is conjoined to "fa-isbir" (so be patient), on the basis that it is a command to patience in the face of the harm of the polytheists.

The naqur (النَّاقُور) is the horn with which the army is summoned, and it is called the ṣūr (الصُّور). It is a large horn or something similar, into which the blower blows to call people who gather to it from an army or the like. Khufaf ibn Nadba said:

When their naqur sounds out one day, people respond from west and east.

Its form is fa'ūl, which is a pattern for the instrument by which the action of naqr (نَقْر, striking/sounding) is performed, and naqr is a sound of the tongue, like a whistle. So His saying nuqira (نُقِرَ) means ṣuwwita (صُوِّتَ), i.e., a sounder sounded. The mention of the ṣūr has already occurred in Surat al-Haqqah.

"Idhā" (إذا) is a noun of time, added to the clause "nuqira fi al-naqur" (نُقِرَ فِي النَّاقُورِ), and it is an adverbial of time. Its governing element is what is indicated by His saying "fa-dhālika yawma'idhin yawmun ʿasīr" (فَذَلِكَ يَوْمَئِذٍ يَوْمٌ عَسِيرٌ), because it contains the force of a verb, meaning: the matter will be difficult for the disbelievers.

The fa' in "fa-dhālika" is the response (jawāb) to "idhā," because "idhā" carries the meaning of a conditional.

The demonstrative refers to what "idhā nuqira" denotes, i.e., that time is a difficult day.

"Yawma'idhin" (يَوْمَئِذٍ) is a substitute (badal) for the demonstrative, serving to clarify the demonstrative in the manner in which a definite noun with "al-" is clarified, as in His saying "dhālika al-kitābu lā rayba fīh" (ذَلِكَ الْكِتَابُ لَا رَيْبَ فِيهِ) [al-Baqarah: 2].

The day is described as difficult by virtue of the hardship that occurs in it for those present in it, so this is a metaphorical attribution in the intellectual sense (wasf majāzī ʿaqlī). Difficulty in reality belongs to the events that take place in it.

"ʿalā al-kāfirīn" (عَلَى الْكَافِرِينَ) is related to "ʿasīr" (عَسِيرٌ).

Describing the day and similar time-nouns by the attributes of the events occurring in them is well known in their speech. Al-Samaw'al, or al-Harithi, said:

Our days are well known among our enemies, with their marks and their white blazes.

The "ghurar" and "ḥujūl" are only metaphorical for the attributes of their encounter with the enemy during their days. In the Thirtieth Maqama: "None has tied this noble knot, on this bright, white-marked day, except the one who roamed and traversed, and grew old in the battle, and turned grey." And the Most High said: "So We sent upon them a furious wind in ominous days" [Fussilat: 16], in Surat Fussilat.

"Ghayru yasīr" (غَيْرُ يَسِيرٍ) is an emphasis on the meaning of "ʿasīr" by its synonym. This is one of the curiosities of usage, as one says "ʿājilan ghayra ājil" (immediately, not deferred). Ṭalib ibn Abi Talib said:

Let the one defeated not be the one who defeats, and let the one plundered not be the one who plunders.

Similar to this, without emphasis, is His saying: "They have indeed gone astray and were not guided" [al-An'am: 140], and "Then I would indeed have gone astray, and I would not be of the guided" [al-An'am: 56]. Al-Zamakhshari pointed out that the benefit of this emphasis is what the word "ghayr" suggests of difference, so it becomes an allusion that for them there is another state, namely ease, i.e., for the believers, so that it combines the threat to the disbelievers and their vexation with the glad tidings for the believers.

Concerning His saying, ﴿Leave Me with the one whom I created alone﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:11], and the rest of the verses. This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) which indicates that an event was the occasion for the revelation of this verse following the verses that precede it. That event was when it spread in Mecca that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had been visited again by revelation after an interval, and that he had been commanded to warn. This is supported by what Ibn Ishaq narrated: that a group of the Quraysh gathered, among them Abu Lahab, Abu Sufyan, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Umayya ibn Khalaf, al-'As ibn Wa'il, and al-Mut'im ibn 'Adi. They said: "The delegations of the Arabs will come to you during the season, and they will ask about the matter of Muhammad, and you have differed in reporting about him. One says he is a madman, another says he is a soothsayer, and another says he is a poet. The Arabs know that all of this does not come together in one man. So name Muhammad by one name on which you agree, and the Arabs will use it." A man among them stood and said: "A poet." Al-Walid ibn al-Mughira said: "I have heard the speech of Ibn al-Abras (meaning 'Ubayd ibn al-Abras) and Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt, and I know all poetry, and the speech of Muhammad does not resemble the speech of a poet." They said: "A soothsayer." Al-Walid said: "It is not the mumbling of a soothsayer, nor his rhymed prose. The soothsayer speaks truth and lies, and Muhammad has never lied at all." Another stood and said: "A madman." Al-Walid said: "We know madness, for the madman is seized with choking, and it is not his choking, nor his convulsions, nor his whisperings." They said: "A sorcerer." Al-Walid said: "We have seen sorcerers and their sorcery, and it is not his blowing (of spittle) nor his knotting." Al-Walid then went back to his house, and Abu Jahl entered upon him and said: "What is wrong with you, O Abu 'Abd Shams? Have you turned away (from your people)?" Al-Walid said: "I have thought about the matter of Muhammad, and the closest thing to say about him is that you say: 'He is a sorcerer who has brought a speech that is sorcery, by which he separates a man from his father, a man from his brother, a man from his wife, and a man from his clan." Ibn Ishaq said: "So God revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira His saying, ﴿Leave Me with the one whom I created alone﴾ and the verses that follow."

[Page 304]

And on the authority of Abu Nasr al-Qushayri, he said: It was said that the statement of the disbelievers of Mecca reached the Prophet (ﷺ): "You are a sorcerer." He felt distress at that and became feverish, so he wrapped himself in his garments. Then God Most High said: ﴿Arise and warn﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:2].

Whatever the case, there is agreement that this statement was made by al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, and that he is the one meant by the saying of God Most High, ﴿and the one whom I created alone﴾. If al-Walid's statement was made after the revelation of the opening of this surah, then the clause ﴿Leave Me with the one whom I created alone﴾ is a fresh, initial resumption, and the connection is clear. If al-Walid's statement was the cause of the revelation of the surah, then it is connected with His saying, ﴿and for your Lord be patient﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:7], as a reason for the command to be patient, namely that God will Himself deal with the recompense of this speaker, and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiradh). This is supported by the fact that the beginning of revelation was in Ramadan, and that the interval of revelation lasted forty days according to the most correct opinion, whether or not revelation came during some days between the beginning of revelation and its interval, or no revelation came after its beginning and its interval occurred. Thus the month of Dhu al-Qa'dah would have been nearing its end, and that is the period when the season draws near. So the polytheists began preparing what they would say to the delegations when they asked them about the news of the Prophet (ﷺ).

The opening of the sentence with the verb (dharni, "leave me") indicates that the Messenger (ﷺ) was concerned and distressed by what al-Walid ibn al-Mughira had fabricated, so its connection with His saying, ﴿and for your Lord be patient﴾ becomes clearer.

What is found in expressions like (dharni, "leave me") and similar, of threat and warning toward the one mentioned after the conjunctive waw (waw al-ma'iyyah, the waw of accompaniment), has already been discussed in the commentary on His saying, Most High, ﴿So leave Me with the one who denies this discourse﴾ [al-Qalam 68:44], in the Surah al-Qalam.

The relative pronoun (man, "the one whom") and its relative clause are used in His saying, ﴿and the one whom I created alone﴾, to incorporate a rebuke of al-Walid's ingratitude for the blessing into the warning and threat.

The word (wahidan, "alone") is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the relative pronoun (man).

Al-wahid means the one who is separate from others in a place or state, as indicated by the context of the speech, or in fame or reputation. It is an intensive form (fa'il) from (wahuda), of the pattern (karuma and 'alima), meaning he became solitary.

Al-Walid ibn al-Mughira was called "the Unique" (al-Wahid) among the Quraysh, because of his singularity and distinction, having gathered together merits that were not gathered by others of his class: a large number of children, abundant wealth, and the glory of himself and his father before him. He was the reference point of the Quraysh in their affairs, because he was older than Abu Jahl and Abu Sufyan. When he became known by the title "the Unique," this statement became an allusion to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, who was known by it. This description came after the verb (khalaqtu, "I created") so as to turn this description away from what was intended by it, so that it would refer to what is suitable to accompany the verb (khalaqtu), meaning: I brought him into being alone, without wealth, children, or ease. Thus the aim shifts from the purpose of praise and commendation, which they used to attribute to him, to the purpose of need for God, which is the state of every created being. It is then of the same kind as His saying, ﴿And God brought you forth from the wombs of your mothers, knowing nothing﴾ [al-Nahl 16:78], and so on.

His saying ﴿and made for him abundant wealth﴾ is conjoined to this by the conjunction (waw) in the manner of conjoining the particular to the general.

Al-mamdud is the passive participle from (madda), which means "to lengthen," in that the abundance of wealth is likened to the vastness of a body's extent. Or it is from (madda) in the sense of "to increase something by its like," as one says: "the valley extended the river," meaning: wealth that is increased in quantity by what its owner gains from earnings. Al-Walid was among the wealthiest of the Quraysh. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: al-Walid's wealth was between Mecca and al-Ta'if, in camels, sheep, slaves, female slaves, and gardens, and the yield of his wealth was a thousand dinars per year.

God bestowed on him the blessing of children, and described them as ("shuhud," "present"), the plural of (shahid, "present"), meaning present, that is, they do not leave him. So he is at ease with them, and his mind is not occupied with their absence or with the fear of the dangers of travel for them. Thus they were free from the need to seek provision through trade or raiding. They used to attend the gatherings with him, so they were a source of pride for him. It was said he had ten sons, and it was said thirteen sons. Those mentioned among them are seven: al-Walid ibn al-Walid, Khalid, 'Umarah, Hisham, al-'As, Qays or Abu Qays, and 'Abd Shams, by whom he was known. Ibn Hazm in Jamharat al-Ansab did not mention al-'As, and limited himself to six.

Al-tamhid is the verbal noun of (mahhada) with the doubled (ha'), which indicates intensity of the (mahd). Al-mahd means leveling the ground and removing what would press on the side of one who lies upon it. The (mahd) of the infant is a naming by the verbal noun.

Al-tamhid here is used metaphorically for facilitating his affairs and the effectiveness of his word among his people, such that no aim is difficult for him and no matter is beyond his reach.

[Page 305]

The verb (mahhadtu, "I made smooth") is emphasized with its own verbal noun as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), so that its indefiniteness may be used to convey the magnitude of that facilitation. It is not necessarily the case that the emphasis is meant to remove the possibility of metaphor.

In this verse he is described with what he possessed of blessing and abundance, because the verse is in the context of bestowing favour upon him, as a preparation for rebuking him and threatening him with evil in this world and with the punishment of the Fire in the Hereafter. As for the verse in Surah al-Qalam, it describes him with the defects he had, in His saying, Most High, ﴿And do not obey every oft-swearing, contemptible one﴾ [al-Qalam 68:10], etc., according to the view of one who says that the intended person is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira (and you have known that this is a possibility), because that verse is in the setting of warning against his evil and treachery.

The (thumma, "then") in His saying ﴿then he is greedy﴾ indicates a rank-based delay (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), meaning: and greater than that is that he is greedy for an increase in those blessings. That is known from the ease of his affairs. This indicates the unlikelihood of what he hopes for being achieved, and this is stated explicitly in His saying, (kalla, "no!").

Greed (al-tama') is seeking a great thing. The object of his greed is made an increase over what God has given him, because they did not attribute provision to the idols, or because it is greed for an increase in blessing without remembering that it is from God. So the attribution of the increase to the divine name (damir al-jalalah) is an incorporation, reminding him that what he is greedy for is from the One whom he disbelieved in regarding His blessing, and so he associated others with Him in worship.

It is for this subtle point that the expression was altered from saying "he is greedy for an increase," or "he is greedy that he be increased."

(Kalla, "no!") is a rebuke and a nullification of his greed for an increase of blessings, and a cutting off of his hope.

The purpose is to convey this to him, along with reassuring the Prophet (ﷺ) that al-Walid will be cut off from the supply of provision, lest his blessing become a trial for others among the opponents, whose condition would encourage them to think that their opposition does not harm them, because they do not expect a life after this one, as God relates from the words of Musa (peace be upon him): ﴿Our Lord, You have given Pharaoh and his chiefs adornment and wealth in the life of this world; our Lord, so that they may lead astray from Your way. Our Lord, obliterate their wealth and harden their hearts, so they will not believe until they see the painful punishment﴾ [Yunus 10:88].

In this nullification and rebuke there is a notice that ingratitude for a blessing is a cause of its being cut off. God Most High said: ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you, but if you are ungrateful, indeed My punishment is severe﴾ [Ibrahim 14:7]. For this reason Shaykh Ibn 'Ata' Allah said: "Whoever does not thank the blessings has exposed them to their loss, and whoever thanks them has bound them with their tether."

Al-wahid means the one who is separate from others in a place or state, as indicated by the context of the speech, or in fame or reputation. It is an intensive form (fa'il) from (wahuda), of the pattern (karuma and 'alima), meaning he became solitary.

Al-Walid ibn al-Mughira was called "the Unique" (al-Wahid) among the Quraysh, because of his singularity and distinction, having gathered together merits that were not gathered by others of his class: a large number of children, abundant wealth, and the glory of himself and his father before him. He was the reference point of the Quraysh in their affairs, because he was older than Abu Jahl and Abu Sufyan. When he became known by the title "the Unique," this statement became an allusion to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, who was known by it. This description came after the verb (khalaqtu, "I created") so as to turn this description away from what was intended by it, so that it would refer to what is suitable to accompany the verb (khalaqtu), meaning: I brought him into being alone, without wealth, children, or ease. Thus the aim shifts from the purpose of praise and commendation, which they used to attribute to him, to the purpose of need for God, which is the state of every created being. It is then of the same kind as His saying, ﴿And God brought you forth from the wombs of your mothers, knowing nothing﴾ [al-Nahl 16:78], and so on.

His saying ﴿and made for him abundant wealth﴾ is conjoined to this by the conjunction (waw) in the manner of conjoining the particular to the general.

Al-mamdud is the passive participle from (madda), which means "to lengthen," in that the abundance of wealth is likened to the vastness of a body's extent. Or it is from (madda) in the sense of "to increase something by its like," as one says: "the valley extended the river," meaning: wealth that is increased in quantity by what its owner gains from earnings. Al-Walid was among the wealthiest of the Quraysh. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: al-Walid's wealth was between Mecca and al-Ta'if, in camels, sheep, slaves, female slaves, and gardens, and the yield of his wealth was a thousand dinars per year.

God bestowed on him the blessing of children, and described them as ("shuhud," "present"), the plural of (shahid, "present"), meaning present, that is, they do not leave him. So he is at ease with them, and his mind is not occupied with their absence or with the fear of the dangers of travel for them. Thus they were free from the need to seek provision through trade or raiding. They used to attend the gatherings with him, so they were a source of pride for him. It was said he had ten sons, and it was said thirteen sons. Those mentioned among them are seven: al-Walid ibn al-Walid, Khalid, 'Umarah, Hisham, al-'As, Qays or Abu Qays, and 'Abd Shams, by whom he was known. Ibn Hazm in Jamharat al-Ansab did not mention al-'As, and limited himself to six.

Al-tamhid is the verbal noun of (mahhada) with the doubled (ha'), which indicates intensity of the (mahd). Al-mahd means leveling the ground and removing what would press on the side of one who lies upon it. The (mahd) of the infant is a naming by the verbal noun.

Al-tamhid here is used metaphorically for facilitating his affairs and the effectiveness of his word among his people, such that no aim is difficult for him and no matter is beyond his reach.

[Page 305]

The verb (mahhadtu, "I made smooth") is emphasized with its own verbal noun as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), so that its indefiniteness may be used to convey the magnitude of that facilitation. It is not necessarily the case that the emphasis is meant to remove the possibility of metaphor.

In this verse he is described with what he possessed of blessing and abundance, because the verse is in the context of bestowing favour upon him, as a preparation for rebuking him and threatening him with evil in this world and with the punishment of the Fire in the Hereafter. As for the verse in Surah al-Qalam, it describes him with the defects he had, in His saying, Most High, ﴿And do not obey every oft-swearing, contemptible one﴾ [al-Qalam 68:10], etc., according to the view of one who says that the intended person is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira (and you have known that this is a possibility), because that verse is in the setting of warning against his evil and treachery.

The (thumma, "then") in His saying ﴿then he is greedy﴾ indicates a rank-based delay (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), meaning: and greater than that is that he is greedy for an increase in those blessings. That is known from the ease of his affairs. This indicates the unlikelihood of what he hopes for being achieved, and this is stated explicitly in His saying, (kalla, "no!").

Greed (al-tama') is seeking a great thing. The object of his greed is made an increase over what God has given him, because they did not attribute provision to the idols, or because it is greed for an increase in blessing without remembering that it is from God. So the attribution of the increase to the divine name (damir al-jalalah) is an incorporation, reminding him that what he is greedy for is from the One whom he disbelieved in regarding His blessing, and so he associated others with Him in worship.

It is for this subtle point that the expression was altered from saying "he is greedy for an increase," or "he is greedy that he be increased."

(Kalla, "no!") is a rebuke and a nullification of his greed for an increase of blessings, and a cutting off of his hope.

The purpose is to convey this to him, along with reassuring the Prophet (ﷺ) that al-Walid will be cut off from the supply of provision, lest his blessing become a trial for others among the opponents, whose condition would encourage them to think that their opposition does not harm them, because they do not expect a life after this one, as God relates from the words of Musa (peace be upon him): ﴿Our Lord, You have given Pharaoh and his chiefs adornment and wealth in the life of this world; our Lord, so that they may lead astray from Your way. Our Lord, obliterate their wealth and harden their hearts, so they will not believe until they see the painful punishment﴾ [Yunus 10:88].

In this nullification and rebuke there is a notice that ingratitude for a blessing is a cause of its being cut off. God Most High said: ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you, but if you are ungrateful, indeed My punishment is severe﴾ [Ibrahim 14:7]. For this reason Shaykh Ibn 'Ata' Allah said: "Whoever does not thank the blessings has exposed them to their loss, and whoever thanks them has bound them with their tether."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 74, verse 16:

Page 306
﴿Indeed, he was stubbornly opposed to Our signs.﴾

It is permissible that this sentence be a causal explanation (ta'lil) of the rebuke and refutation, meaning: because his intense opposition to Our signs was ingratitude for the blessing, it was therefore a cause for its being withdrawn from him, since he had exceeded the limit of disbelief into hostility and obstinate opposition. For the disbeliever is one upon whom blessing has been bestowed, according to the preferred view, and this is the opinion of al-Maturidi and the Mu'tazilah, in contrast to al-Ash'ari. The verifying scholars (al-muhaqqiqun) held that this is a verbal disagreement (khilaf lafzi).

It is also permissible that the sentence be a new, independent statement (mustana'fah), and the pause would then be at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Kalla﴾ (No).

Al-'Anid (the stubborn one): one who is extremely obstinate, and this is opposition to what is correct. It is on the pattern fa'il from 'anada, ya'nidu, like darab, when he disputes with and argues against the clear truth.

His obstinacy is his attempt to attack the Qur'an and to devise (tahyil) for it, misleading people by claiming that it is magic, or poetry, or the speech of soothsaying, while being certain that there is nothing of that in it, as he himself declared to the Quraysh, before Abu Jahl rebuked him and then he took hold of one of those three, which is that he said: it is magic, clinging to the claim that it has the characteristics of magic in separating a man from one who is closely bound to him.

[Page 307]

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Taḥrīr wa'l-Tanwīr) on Sūrah 74, verses 17–25:**

﴿I will overwhelm him with a rugged ascent.﴾ ﴿Indeed, he thought and calculated.﴾ ﴿So may he be destroyed, how he calculated!﴾ ﴿Again, may he be destroyed, how he calculated!﴾ ﴿Then he looked.﴾ ﴿Then he frowned and scowled.﴾ ﴿Then he turned away and was arrogant.﴾ ﴿And he said, "This is nothing but magic, transmitted from others."﴾ ﴿"This is nothing but the word of a human being."﴾

The sentence ﴿I will overwhelm him with a rugged ascent﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ) between ﴿Indeed, he was hostile to Our signs﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 16] and ﴿Indeed, he thought and calculated﴾. By this parenthetical insertion, the purpose is to hasten the threat against him as a source of distress for him, and to hasten good news for the Prophet (ﷺ).

The sentence ﴿Indeed, he thought and calculated﴾ explains the sentence ﴿Indeed, he was hostile to Our signs﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 16]. So it completes and clarifies it.

*Al-irhāq* (overwhelming) means causing exhaustion and imposing what cannot be borne. Its verb is *rahiqa*, like *firiḥa*. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And do not overwhelm me with difficulty in my affair﴾ [al-Kahf: 73], in Sūrat al-Kahf.

*Al-ṣaʿūd* is a steep incline, very hard to climb, difficult for the one walking on it. It is an intensive form (*faʿūl*, form of hyperbole) from *ṣaʿida*, for an incline is *ṣaʿda*. When an incline is steeper in its climbing than the usual inclines, it is called *ṣaʿūd*.

It seems that the origin of this description is that the incline was described as "ascending" by way of rational metaphor (*majāz ʿaqlī*, attributing an action to something other than its true agent). Then this description became a generic noun for it.

His saying ﴿I will overwhelm him with a rugged ascent﴾ is an image representing the opposite of the state summarized in His saying ﴿And I furnished for him [wealth] abundantly﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 14]. That is: his condition will change from a state of ease and luxury to a wretched state in this world, and then to painful punishment in the Hereafter. All of that is overwhelming for him.

It has been said that his death throes will be prolonged, so that his soul will keep ascending without him dying, and he will be given from the torment of the Fire what the torment of this world leads to.

His threat has been distributed according to what his deeds require. When his hostility was mentioned, which stems from his evil aims arising from his guarding of his leadership and from his envy of the Prophet (ﷺ), and these are worldly purposes, he was followed by a threat that includes the torment of this world first. And when his slander against the Qur'an was mentioned in His saying ﴿This is nothing but magic, transmitted from others﴾, and he denied that it is revelation from God in His saying ﴿This is nothing but the word of a human being﴾, it was followed by mention of the punishment of the Hereafter in His saying ﴿I will burn him in Saqar﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 26].

It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that: "Ṣaʿūd is a mountain in Hell, one ascends it for seventy autumns, then one falls down from it, and so on forever." Narrated by al-Tirmidhī and Aḥmad from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī. Al-Tirmidhī said: "It is a strange (gharīb) ḥadīth." So God made the description ṣaʿūd a proper name for that mountain in Hell. This is an interpretation with the greatest of what the Exalted saying ﴿I will overwhelm him with a rugged ascent﴾ indicates.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, he thought and calculated﴾ through to its end is a substitute (badal) for the sentence ﴿Indeed, he was hostile to Our signs﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 16], a substitution of comprehensive inclusion (*badal ishtimāl*), meaning that it includes the earlier statement in a general sense.

He described his state in his hesitation and contemplation in the most eloquent description. It began with mention of his thinking about the opinion he would issue and his calculating of it.

The meaning of ﴿thought﴾ (*fakkara*) is that he applied his thought and repeatedly examined his opinion in order to devise an excuse that he could disguise and promote among the common people, by describing the Qur'an with the description of human speech, so as to remove from them the belief that it is revelation sent down to the Prophet (ﷺ).

(*Qaddara*, "calculated") means that he set a measure for what came to his mind regarding how to describe the Qur'an, so that he could present it according to what suits the kinds of human speech that the Qur'an attributes to them, or what he marks the Prophet (ﷺ) with from people whose states differ from the usual states of people. An example of that: he says to himself, "Let us say: Muḥammad is a madman." Then he says: "The madman is choked, convulsed and whispers, and Muḥammad is not like that." Then he says to himself: "He is a poet." So he says to himself: "I have known poetry and heard the speech of poets, and Muḥammad's speech does not resemble the speech of a poet." Then he says: "He is a soothsayer." So he says to himself: "His speech is not the mumbling of a soothsayer, nor his rhymed prose." Then he says to himself: "Let us say he is a sorcerer, for magic separates a man from his kin, and Muḥammad separates a man from his wife, his child and his clients." So he said to the people: "We say he is a sorcerer." This is the meaning of ﴿calculated﴾.

His saying ﴿So may he be destroyed, how he calculated!﴾ is a parenthetical statement between ﴿thought﴾ and ﴿calculated﴾ and between ﴿Then he looked﴾. It is a performative statement (*inshāʾ*) of cursing, branched off from the report that he thought and calculated, because what has been mentioned necessitates anger against him.

So the particle *fa* (then/so) is for deriving his censure from his evil act. Similar to it in parenthetical use is His saying: ﴿And We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed. So ask the people of the reminder if you do not know, with clear proofs and scriptures﴾ [al-Naḥl: 43].

Branching does not contradict parenthetical insertion, because parenthetical insertion is placing speech between two connected statements, regardless of what the parenthetical speech is composed of, for that proceeds according to what its meaning requires. The motive for the parenthetical insertion is to hasten the benefit of the speech, to give it importance. Those who claimed that a parenthetical insertion cannot be with *fa* have been mistaken.

*Qutila* (may he be destroyed) is a supplication against him that a slayer may kill him, meaning a supplication against him for his death to be hastened, because his life is an evil life. This supplication is used to express wonder at his condition and lament for him, like the saying "May God fight them" (*qātalahumu Allāh*), and the saying "May you be bereft" (*ʿadimtuka*) and "May his mother be bereaved of him" (*thakilat-hu ummuhu*). It may also be used similarly to express wonder at a good condition, as one says: "May God fight him, how brave he is!" Al-Zamakhsharī made it a metonymy (*kināyah*) for his having reached a level that the speaker envies him for, to the point that he wishes him death. I think that the meaning of envy is not intended; rather this is merely a restriction to what that expression contains of wonder or of making wonder, because it has become like proverbs in that respect. The context here clearly requires a metonymy for the badness of his condition, because what he calculated is not something for which people of intellect would envy him for reaching, since he contradicted his own earlier statement when he said: "It is not a spell of sorcerers, nor their blowing," and after he thought, he said: "This is nothing but magic, transmitted from others," so he contradicted himself.

His saying ﴿Again, may he be destroyed, how he calculated!﴾ is an emphasis of its parallel that was branched with *fa*. The conjunction with *thumma* (then, again) indicates that its clause is higher in rank than the one before it in the purpose the speech is directed toward. When the conjoined thing is the same as the one it is conjoined to, it indicates that the meaning of the earlier item has degrees of varying intensity, and emphasis gives the speech strength. This is like His saying: ﴿No! They will soon know. Again, no! They will soon know﴾ [al-Naba': 4–5].

*Kayfa qaddara* ("how he calculated") in both places has one meaning. It is an interrogative noun denoting the state that its complement (what follows *kayfa*) specifies.

The interrogation is directed at an unspecified listener, the speaker asking his listener about the state of his calculating. It is an interrogation used to express wonder mixed with denunciation, by way of figurative speech (*majāz mursal*, metonymy in a broader sense).

*Kayfa* is in the position of an accusative of circumstance (*ḥāl*), placed before its referent, because it has the right of initial position, and its governing element is *qaddara*.

His saying ﴿Then he looked﴾, ﴿Then he frowned and scowled﴾, and ﴿Then he turned away and was arrogant﴾ are conjoined to ﴿and calculated﴾. They are a successive escalation in what calls for wonder at his state and denunciation of him. The delay here is a delay of rank, not of time, because his looking, frowning, scowling, turning away and arrogance accompany his thinking and calculating.

*Al-naẓar* here is looking with the eye, so that it adds to what ﴿thought and calculated﴾ conveys. The meaning is: he looked at the faces of those present, drawing out their opinions on how to ascribe to the Qur'an what they describe it as.

*ʿAbasa* means he contracted his face when what he describes the Qur'an with became difficult for him, and he did not find an acceptable point of attack.

*Basara* means his face became contorted and its color changed, out of fear and grief, when he found nothing to relieve his thirst of a critique of the Qur'an that minds would not reject. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Faces that Day will be gloomy﴾ [al-Qiyāmah: 24], ﴿Expecting that there will be done to them a calamity that breaks the spine﴾ [al-Qiyāmah: 25], in Sūrat al-Qiyāmah.

*Al-idbār* (turning away) here may be a metaphor for the change in the thinking that he was contemplating and calculating, out of despair of finding what he had thought up to ascribe, so he turned to arrogance and disdain at bearing witness to the Qur'an for what it contains of perfection of word and meaning. It may also be a metaphor for increasing his aversion from confirming the Prophet (ﷺ), like the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Then he turned away, striving﴾ [al-Nāziʿāt: 22], relating about Pharaoh, in Sūrat al-Nāziʿāt.

The forms he took on, when he exhausted himself in deriving what he would describe the Qur'an with, are described, and that is mockery of al-Walīd.

The form of restriction (*ṣīghat al-ḥaṣr*) in His saying ﴿This is nothing but magic, transmitted from others﴾ indicates that the inquiry into the states of the Qur'an, after examination and division, led him to conclude that it is of the category of magic. So it is a restriction of specification (*qaṣr taʿyīn*) to one of the sayings that circulated in his mind, because he said: "It is not the speech of a poet, nor the speech of a soothsayer, nor the speech of a madman," as was mentioned in his report.

He described this magic as *maʾthūr* (transmitted), meaning related from the ancients. He says this to ward off an objection against him, that the speech and actions of sorcerers are not similar to the Qur'an, nor to the Messenger's circumstances, so he claimed that it is magical speech, unfamiliar in kind.

The sentence ﴿This is nothing but the word of a human being﴾ is a substitute of comprehensive inclusion (*badal ishtimāl*) for the sentence ﴿This is nothing but magic, transmitted from others﴾, in that magic can be speech and actions, so this is verbal magic. This sentence stands in the position of a conclusion to what preceded, because his intent from all of that is that the Qur'an is not revelation from God.

He conjoined his saying ﴿Then he said﴾ with *fa* (then), because when this utterance occurred to him after the thorough working of his thought, he could not restrain himself from uttering it, so his uttering it was fittingly conjoined with a particle of sequence.

It has been said that his death throes will be prolonged, so that his soul will keep ascending without him dying, and he will be given from the torment of the Fire what the torment of this world leads to.

His threat has been distributed according to what his deeds require. When his hostility was mentioned, which stems from his evil aims arising from his guarding of his leadership and from his envy of the Prophet (ﷺ), and these are worldly purposes, he was followed by a threat that includes the torment of this world first. Then he says: "He is a soothsayer." So he says to himself: "His speech is not the mumbling of a soothsayer, nor his rhymed prose." The sentence ﴿Indeed, he thought and calculated﴾ explains the sentence ﴿Indeed, he was hostile to Our signs﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 16]. So it completes and clarifies it.

It seems that the origin of this description is that the incline was described as "ascending" by way of rational metaphor (*majāz ʿaqlī*, attributing an action to something other than its true agent). Then this description became a generic noun for it.

His saying ﴿I will overwhelm him with a rugged ascent﴾ is an image representing the opposite of the state summarized in His saying ﴿And I furnished for him [wealth] abundantly﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 14]. That is: his condition will change from a state of ease and luxury to a wretched state in this world, and then to painful punishment in the Hereafter. All of that is overwhelming for him.

It has been said that his death throes will be prolonged, so that his soul will keep ascending without him dying, and he will be given from the torment of the Fire what the torment of this world leads to.

His threat has been distributed according to what his deeds require. When his hostility was mentioned, which stems from his evil aims arising from his guarding of his leadership and from his envy of the Prophet (ﷺ), and these are worldly purposes, he was followed by a threat that includes the torment of this world first. And when his slander against the Qur'an was mentioned in His saying ﴿This is nothing but magic, transmitted from others﴾, and he denied that it is revelation from God in His saying ﴿This is nothing but the word of a human being﴾, it was followed by mention of the punishment of the Hereafter in His saying ﴿I will burn him in Saqar﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 26].

It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that: "Ṣaʿūd is a mountain in Hell, one ascends it for seventy autumns, then one falls down from it, and so on forever." Narrated by al-Tirmidhī and Aḥmad from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī. Al-Tirmidhī said: "It is a strange (gharīb) ḥadīth." So God made the description ṣaʿūd a proper name for that mountain in Hell. This is an interpretation with the greatest of what the Exalted saying ﴿I will overwhelm him with a rugged ascent﴾ indicates.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, he thought and calculated﴾ through to its end is a substitute (badal) for the sentence ﴿Indeed, he was hostile to Our signs﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 16], a substitution of comprehensive inclusion (*badal ishtimāl*), meaning that it includes the earlier statement in a general sense.

He described his state in his hesitation and contemplation in the most eloquent description. It began with mention of his thinking about the opinion he would issue and his calculating of it.

The meaning of ﴿thought﴾ (*fakkara*) is that he applied his thought and repeatedly examined his opinion in order to devise an excuse that he could disguise and promote among the common people, by describing the Qur'an with the description of human speech, so as to remove from them the belief that it is revelation sent down to the Prophet (ﷺ).

(*Qaddara*, "calculated") means that he set a measure for what came to his mind regarding how to describe the Qur'an, so that he could present it according to what suits the kinds of human speech that the Qur'an attributes to them, or what he marks the Prophet (ﷺ) with from people whose states differ from the usual states of people. An example of that: he says to himself, "Let us say: Muḥammad is a madman." Then he says: "The madman is choked, convulsed and whispers, and Muḥammad is not like that." Then he says to himself: "He is a poet." So he says to himself: "I have known poetry and heard the speech of poets, and Muḥammad's speech does not resemble the speech of a poet." Then he says: "He is a soothsayer." So he says to himself: "His speech is not the mumbling of a soothsayer, nor his rhymed prose." Then he says to himself: "Let us say he is a sorcerer, for magic separates a man from his kin, and Muḥammad separates a man from his wife, his child and his clients." So he said to the people: "We say he is a sorcerer." This is the meaning of ﴿calculated﴾.

His saying ﴿So may he be destroyed, how he calculated!﴾ is a parenthetical statement between ﴿thought﴾ and ﴿calculated﴾ and between ﴿Then he looked﴾. It is a performative statement (*inshāʾ*) of cursing, branched off from the report that he thought and calculated, because what has been mentioned necessitates anger against him.

So the particle *fa* (then/so) is for deriving his censure from his evil act. Similar to it in parenthetical use is His saying: ﴿And We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed. So ask the people of the reminder if you do not know, with clear proofs and scriptures﴾ [al-Naḥl: 43].

Branching does not contradict parenthetical insertion, because parenthetical insertion is placing speech between two connected statements, regardless of what the parenthetical speech is composed of, for that proceeds according to what its meaning requires. The motive for the parenthetical insertion is to hasten the benefit of the speech, to give it importance. Those who claimed that a parenthetical insertion cannot be with *fa* have been mistaken.

*Qutila* (may he be destroyed) is a supplication against him that a slayer may kill him, meaning a supplication against him for his death to be hastened, because his life is an evil life. This supplication is used to express wonder at his condition and lament for him, like the saying "May God fight them" (*qātalahumu Allāh*), and the saying "May you be bereft" (*ʿadimtuka*) and "May his mother be bereaved of him" (*thakilat-hu ummuhu*). It may also be used similarly to express wonder at a good condition, as one says: "May God fight him, how brave he is!" Al-Zamakhsharī made it a metonymy (*kināyah*) for his having reached a level that the speaker envies him for, to the point that he wishes him death. I think that the meaning of envy is not intended; rather this is merely a restriction to what that expression contains of wonder or of making wonder, because it has become like proverbs in that respect. The context here clearly requires a metonymy for the badness of his condition, because what he calculated is not something for which people of intellect would envy him for reaching, since he contradicted his own earlier statement when he said: "It is not a spell of sorcerers, nor their blowing," and after he thought, he said: "This is nothing but magic, transmitted from others," so he contradicted himself.

His saying ﴿Again, may he be destroyed, how he calculated!﴾ is an emphasis of its parallel that was branched with *fa*. The conjunction with *thumma* (then, again) indicates that its clause is higher in rank than the one before it in the purpose the speech is directed toward. When the conjoined thing is the same as the one it is conjoined to, it indicates that the meaning of the earlier item has degrees of varying intensity, and emphasis gives the speech strength. This is like His saying: ﴿No! They will soon know. Again, no! They will soon know﴾ [al-Naba': 4–5].

The interrogation is directed at an unspecified listener, the speaker asking his listener about the state of his calculating. It is an interrogation used to express wonder mixed with denunciation, by way of figurative speech (*majāz mursal*, metonymy in a broader sense).

*Kayfa* is in the position of an accusative of circumstance (*ḥāl*), placed before its referent, because it has the right of initial position, and its governing element is *qaddara*.

His saying ﴿Then he looked﴾, ﴿Then he frowned and scowled﴾, and ﴿Then he turned away and was arrogant﴾ are conjoined to ﴿and calculated﴾. They are a successive escalation in what calls for wonder at his state and denunciation of him. The delay here is a delay of rank, not of time, because his looking, frowning, scowling, turning away and arrogance accompany his thinking and calculating.

*Al-naẓar* here is looking with the eye, so that it adds to what ﴿thought and calculated﴾ conveys. The meaning is: he looked at the faces of those present, drawing out their opinions on how to ascribe to the Qur'an what they describe it as.

*ʿAbasa* means he contracted his face when what he describes the Qur'an with became difficult for him, and he did not find an acceptable point of attack.

*Basara* means his face became contorted and its color changed, out of fear and grief, when he found nothing to relieve his thirst of a critique of the Qur'an that minds would not reject. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Faces that Day will be gloomy﴾ [al-Qiyāmah: 24], ﴿Expecting that there will be done to them a calamity that breaks the spine﴾ [al-Qiyāmah: 25], in Sūrat al-Qiyāmah.

*Al-idbār* (turning away) here may be a metaphor for the change in the thinking that he was contemplating and calculating, out of despair of finding what he had thought up to ascribe, so he turned to arrogance and disdain at bearing witness to the Qur'an for what it contains of perfection of word and meaning. It may also be a metaphor for increasing his aversion from confirming the Prophet (ﷺ), like the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Then he turned away, striving﴾ [al-Nāziʿāt: 22], relating about Pharaoh, in Sūrat al-Nāziʿāt.

The form of restriction (*ṣīghat al-ḥaṣr*) in His saying ﴿This is nothing but magic, transmitted from others﴾ indicates that the inquiry into the states of the Qur'an, after examination and division, led him to conclude that it is of the category of magic. He described this magic as *maʾthūr* (transmitted), meaning related from the ancients. He says this to ward off an objection against him, that the speech and actions of sorcerers are not similar to the Qur'an, nor to the Messenger's circumstances, so he claimed that it is magical speech, unfamiliar in kind.

The sentence ﴿This is nothing but the word of a human being﴾ is a substitute of comprehensive inclusion (*badal ishtimāl*) for the sentence ﴿This is nothing but magic, transmitted from others﴾, in that magic can be speech and actions, so this is verbal magic. This sentence stands in the position of a conclusion to what preceded, because his intent from all of that is that the Qur'an is not revelation from God.

He conjoined his saying ﴿Then he said﴾ with *fa* (then), because when this utterance occurred to him after the thorough working of his thought, he could not restrain himself from uttering it, so his uttering it was fittingly conjoined with a particle of sequence.

God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Faces that Day will be gloomy﴾ [al-Qiyāmah: 24], ﴿Expecting that there will be done to them a calamity that breaks the spine﴾ [al-Qiyāmah: 25], in Sūrat al-Qiyāmah.

*Al-idbār* (turning away) here may be a metaphor for the change in the thinking that he was contemplating and calculating, out of despair of finding what he had thought up to ascribe, so he turned to arrogance and disdain at bearing witness to the Qur'an for what it contains of perfection of word and meaning. It may also be a metaphor for increasing his aversion from confirming the Prophet (ﷺ), like the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Then he turned away, striving﴾ [al-Nāziʿāt: 22], relating about Pharaoh, in Sūrat al-Nāziʿāt.

The forms he took on, when he exhausted himself in deriving what he would describe the Qur'an with, are described, and that is mockery of al-Walīd.

The form of restriction (*ṣīghat al-ḥaṣr*) in His saying ﴿This is nothing but magic, transmitted from others﴾ indicates that the inquiry into the states of the Qur'an, after examination and division, led him to conclude that it is of the category of magic. So it is a restriction of specification (*qaṣr taʿyīn*) to one of the sayings that circulated in his mind, because he said: "It is not the speech of a poet, nor the speech of a soothsayer, nor the speech of a madman," as was mentioned in his report.

He described this magic as *maʾthūr* (transmitted), meaning related from the ancients. He says this to ward off an objection against him, that the speech and actions of sorcerers are not similar to the Qur'an, nor to the Messenger's circumstances, so he claimed that it is magical speech, unfamiliar in kind.

The sentence ﴿This is nothing but the word of a human being﴾ is a substitute of comprehensive inclusion (*badal ishtimāl*) for the sentence ﴿This is nothing but magic, transmitted from others﴾, in that magic can be speech and actions, so this is verbal magic. This sentence stands in the position of a conclusion to what preceded, because his intent from all of that is that the Qur'an is not revelation from God.

He conjoined his saying ﴿Then he said﴾ with *fa* (then), because when this utterance occurred to him after the thorough working of his thought, he could not restrain himself from uttering it, so his uttering it was fittingly conjoined with a particle of sequence.

The sentence ﴿سَأُصْلِيهِ سَقَرَ﴾ ("I shall cast him into Saqar") is a resumptive clause (istiʼnaf bayani, a clause that answers an implied question) arising from His saying ﴿إنَّهُ فَكَّرَ وقَدَّرَ﴾ ("Indeed, he reflected and calculated") [al-Muddaththir: 18] through to the end of the verses. It mentions His threat of the punishment of the Hereafter.

It may also be a substitute (badal) for the clause ﴿سَأُصْلِيهِ سَقَرَ﴾. The verb iṣlāʼ (إصلاء) means causing something to be exposed to (ṣāliyan, صالِيًا), that is, directly experiencing the heat of the fire. The verb ṣalā (صَلِيَ) is used for feeling the heat of a fire, in which case it is for the purpose of warming oneself, as in the words of al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥillizah:

*fatanawwarta nārahā min baʻīdin bi-Khazāzā ayyāna minka al-ṣilāʼu*
"So you looked upon its fire from afar, at Khazaza; where, from you, is the warming?"
That is, you are far from warming yourself by it.

As Ḥumayd ibn Thawr said:

*lā taṣṭalī al-nāra illā mijmaran arijā*
*qad kassarta min yalanjūjin lahu waqaṣā*
"You do not warm yourself at the fire except at a fragrant brazier, of which you have broken pieces of aloeswood and its stalks."

The verb is also used for being burned by fire. Allah says ﴿سَيَصْلى نارًا ذاتَ لَهَبٍ﴾ ("He will enter a Fire of blazing flame") [al-Masad: 3] in the surah of Abu Lahab; He says ﴿فَأنْذَرْتُكم نارًا تَلَظّى﴾ ("I have warned you of a Fire that blazes") [al-Layl: 14] and ﴿لا يَصْلاها إلّا الأشْقى﴾ ("None will enter it except the most wretched") [al-Layl: 15] in the surah of al-Layl; and He says ﴿وسَيَصْلَوْنَ سَعِيرًا﴾ ("And they will enter a Blaze") [al-Nisa': 10] in the surah of al-Nisa'. When this root is followed by a second object that is one of the names of the Fire, the verb most often means burning, as in His saying ﴿فَسَوْفَ نُصْلِيهِ نارًا﴾ ("We will surely cast him into the Fire") [al-Nisa': 30] in the surah of al-Nisa'. From this is His saying here ﴿سَأُصْلِيهِ سَقَرَ﴾.

Saqar (سَقَرُ) is a proper name for a level of Jahannam (Hell). It is reported from Ibn ʻAbbas that it is the sixth level of Jahannam. Ibn ʻAṭiyyah said: "Saqar is the sixth level (darak) of Jahannam, according to what has been narrated," end quote. Ibn ʻAṭiyyah restricted himself to this. The statements of the majority of the exegetes imply that they explain Saqar by a term synonymous with Jahannam.

Saqar is diptotic (mamnuʻ min al-ṣarf), because of definiteness as a proper name (ʻalamiyyah) and feminine gender, since it is the name of a region of Jahannam or the name of Jahannam itself. The pronoun referring to (Saqar) is feminine in His saying, "It does not let anything remain" up to His saying ﴿عَلَيْها تِسْعَةَ عَشَرَ﴾ ("Over it are nineteen"). It has been said that Saqar is a loanword (muʻarrab). Al-Suyuti, in al-Itqan, transmitted this from al-Jawaliqi, but he did not mention the word nor from which language it comes.

The clause ﴿وما أدْراكَ ما سَقَرُ﴾ ("And what can make you know what Saqar is?") is a circumstantial clause (ḥāliyyah) referring to (Saqar): that is, Saqar, whose state no informant can inform you of. This is an expression of the awfulness of its condition.

(Mā saqar, ما سَقَرُ) is in the position of a subject (mubtada'), and its original form is "Saqar mā", meaning "what it is". The (mā) was fronted because it is an interrogative particle, which has the right to begin the sentence.

The first (mā) is interrogative. The meaning is: "What thing makes you know, that is, informs you?"

The second (mā) is also interrogative, in the position of a predicate (khabar) about (Saqar).

The clause ﴿لا تُبْقِي﴾ ("It does not let anything remain") is an inclusive apposition (badal ishtimal) of the awfulness expressed by the clause ﴿وما أدْراكَ ما سَقَرُ﴾, since among its horrors is that it destroys everyone who enters it. The clause is a second predicate about (Saqar).

The object of (تُبْقِي, lets remain) is omitted for the purpose of generality: that is, it does not leave any of them alive, or it does not leave any part of their bodies intact.

The clause ﴿ولا تَذَرُ﴾ ("nor does it spare") is coordinated with ﴿لا تُبْقِي﴾, so it has the sense of a circumstantial clause. The meaning of ﴿لا تَذَرُ﴾ is that it does not leave whoever is cast into it, that is, it does not leave him unburned by its punishment. This is a metonymy (kināyah) for restoring his life after it has destroyed him, as Allah says ﴿كُلَّما نَضِجَتْ جُلُودُهم بَدَّلْناهم جُلُودًا غَيْرَها لِيَذُوقُوا العَذابَ﴾ ("Whenever their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins so they may taste the punishment") [al-Nisa': 56].

﴿لَوّاحَةٌ﴾ ("Scorching the skin") is a third predicate about (Saqar). (Lawwāḥah) is of the form faʻʻālah, from al-lawḥ, which is a change in the essence (of a thing) due to pain or the like. A poet, whose verse is among the evidences cited in al-Kashshaf, and whose speaker I have not identified, said:

*taqūlu mā lāḥaka yā musāfir*
*yā ibnata ʻammī lāḥanī al-hawājir*
"She says: 'What has changed you, O traveler? O daughter of my paternal uncle, the noon heat has changed me.'"

(Al-bashar, البَشَرُ) may be the plural of (bashrah), which is the human skin, meaning that it changes the colors of the skins, making them black. It may also be a collective noun (ism jamʻ) for people, having no singular from its own form.

His saying ﴿عَلَيْها تِسْعَةَ عَشَرَ﴾ ("Over it are nineteen") is a fourth predicate about (Saqar) from His saying ﴿وما أدْراكَ ما سَقَرُ﴾.

The meaning of (ʻalayhā, over it) is "in charge of its guarding". Thus (ʻalā, over) is for figurative elevation, comparing authority and governance to elevation, as one says: "So-and-so is over the police" or "over the treasury," meaning he is in charge of that. The meaning is that the guardians of Saqar are nineteen angels.

A group said that the number nineteen refers to the chiefs of the angels appointed over Jahannam.

It was also said that they are nineteen categories of angels, and it was said that they are nineteen ranks. In the tafsir of al-Fakhr (al-Razi), he said: "The people of meanings have mentioned several explanations for this number. One of them is the saying of the people of wisdom: the cause of the corruption of the soul is the animal and natural faculties. As for the animal faculties, they are the five outward senses and the five inward senses, plus desire and anger, which together total twelve. As for the natural faculties, they are the attractive, the retentive, the digestive, the expulsive, the nutritive, the growth-producing, and the generative faculties. These are seven. Perhaps each of these levels is assigned to the people of a branch of disbelief.
