Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 74, verse 31 (part 1 of 2):

﴿We have appointed none as the guardians of the Fire except angels, and We have made their number only a trial for those who disbelieve, so that those who were given the Scripture may become certain, and those who believe may increase in faith, and those who were given the Scripture and the believers may not doubt, and so that those in whose hearts is a disease and the disbelievers may say, "What did Allah intend by this as an example?"﴾ Al-Tabari reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Jabir ibn Zayd that when Abu Jahl heard the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿Over it are nineteen﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 30], he said to the Quraysh: "May your mothers be bereaved! Ibn Abi Kabshah tells you that the guardians of the Fire are nineteen, and you are the multitude! Can it be that every ten of you cannot overpower a single man from the guardians of Hell?" Then Allah the Exalted said, ﴿We have appointed none as the guardians of the Fire except angels﴾, meaning: We have not made them men, so that each man would seize a man; so who can overpower the angels? End of quotation.

[Page 314]

In the Tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis) of al-Qurtubi, on the authority of al-Suddi, it is related that Abu al-Ashaddd ibn Kaladah al-Jumahi said mockingly: "Let not the nineteen frighten you. I will push ten away with my right shoulder and nine with my left shoulder, and then you will pass through into Paradise." It is also said that al-Harith ibn Kaladah said: "I will suffice for you seventeen, and you suffice me with two," intending mockery while displaying the extent of his strength among his people.

Thus, what is meant by "the companions of the Fire" is its guardians, who were mentioned earlier in His words, ﴿Over it are nineteen﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 30].

The exception is from the general category of kinds: that is, We did not make the guardians of the Fire of any kind except the kind of angels.

The form of restriction (qasr) serves to reverse the belief of Abu Jahl and others, who imagined, or pretended to imagine, that the intended meaning was nineteen men, and so they hoped that they themselves and their companions could escape from them by force. Abu al-Ashaddd ibn Usayd al-Jumahi said: "They will not reach my garment until I push them away from Jahannam," that is, until I drive them off.

His words, ﴿We have made their number only a trial for those who disbelieve﴾, are a supplement that refutes the polytheists' supposition that the number of the guardians of the Fire is small. This is a statement following the rhetorical method of wise discourse, since the speech had stirred in souls a question about the purpose of making the guardians of Hell nineteen, and why they were not thousands, so that their sight would be more terrifying to the people of the Fire, or why they were not a single angel, since the powers of the angels accomplish every task Allah subjects them to. The answer to this question is that this number has revealed to the various classes of people the extent of the disbelievers' understanding of the Qur'an. The trial arose only from the mention of their number in the preceding verse. Thus His words, ﴿We have made their number﴾, are to be understood as: We have made the mention of their number only a trial. And it is for the certainty of those who were given the Scripture, the increase of faith in those who believe, and the agitation of those in whose hearts is a disease, so that the misguidance of the misguided and the guidance of the guided become manifest. Allah made the number of the guardians of the Fire nineteen for another wisdom, other than what is mentioned here, which required that arrangement, and which Allah knows.

The exception is a derived exception (istithna' mufarragh) for the second object of the verb ja'ala ("made"). The meaning is: We made their number a trial and nothing more. Since the trial is a state affecting those who disbelieve, it was not intended in itself, but rather its occurrence to those who disbelieve; so it is a circumstance for them.

[Page 315]

The full sense is: We did not make the mention of their number, for any cause or purpose, except for the purpose of the trial of those who disbelieve. Thus (fitnatan, "a trial") is in the accusative as a second object of the verb ja'ala in the derived exception. This is a restriction turned around to answer those who disbelieve, since they believed that their number was a trivial matter.

His words, ﴿so that those who were given the Scripture may become certain﴾, etc., are a second cause of the verb in ﴿We have made their number only a trial﴾. Were it not that the word (fitnah, "trial") is in the accusative as the direct object of the verb ja'ala, the correct construction for (li-yastayqina, "so that he may become certain") would be to be coordinated with (fitnatan), but it has come in the structure of the speech as dependent on the verb in ﴿We have made their number only a trial﴾.

It is also permissible that (lillatheena kafaru, "for those who disbelieve") be dependent on both the verb ja'ala and on (fitnatan), by way of the grammatical dispute (tanazu'), meaning: We did not make their number for those who disbelieve except as a trial for them, since from the mention of it they gained nothing but corruption of interpretation; and that number is made for other benefits for those other than those who disbelieve, who entrust knowledge of that to the knowledge of Allah and to a beneficial reflection.

Al-istiyqan (certainty) is the strength of certainty; the sin and ta' in it are for intensification. The meaning is: so that they may be certain of the truth of the Qur'an, since they find this number confirming what is in their books.

What is meant by "those who were given the Scripture" is the Jews, when what is in the Qur'an reaches them that is like what is in their books or traditions. The Jews used to travel to Mecca for trade, and the people of Mecca used to come to them for provisions in Khaybar, Qurayzah, and Yathrib. So some of them would ask one another about what Muhammad ﷺ was saying, and the polytheists would wish to find with the Jews something with which they could deny the reports of the Qur'an; but they did not find it, and had they found it, it would have been the easiest thing for them to use to attack the Qur'an.

Certainty, by its nature, is followed by faith when it meets a sound intellect free from the impediments of disbelief, as happened to 'Abd Allah ibn Salam. But it may not be followed by faith, due to obstinacy, envy, or fear of losing rank or wealth, as was the case with many of the Jews, about whom Allah said, ﴿They recognize it as they recognize their own sons, and indeed a group of them conceal the truth while they know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 146]. For this reason the verse limited itself to the attainment of certainty by them.

Al-Tirmidhi related with his chain (sanad, the chain of transmission) to Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "Some Jews said to some of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ: 'Does your Prophet know the number of the guardians of the Fire?' They said: 'We do not know until we ask our Prophet.' A man came to the Prophet and said: 'O Muhammad, your companions have been defeated today.'"

[Page 316]

He said: "And how were they defeated?" He said: "The Jews asked them: 'Does your Prophet know the number of the guardians of the Fire?' He said: 'And what did they say?' He said: 'They said, "We do not know until we ask our Prophet."' He said: 'Has a people been defeated when they were asked about what they do not know?' Then they said: 'We do not know until we ask our Prophet.'" [Jabir] continued until he said: "When they came, they said: 'O Abu al-Qasim, how many are the guardians of Jahannam?' He said: 'Like this and like this,' once ten, and once ten, and once nine, indicating with his fingers. They said: 'Yes,'" etc. There is nothing in this that compels us to regard this verse as having been revealed in Medina, as was reported from Qatadah, because the back-and-forth between the polytheists and the Jews about the reports of the Qur'an was familiar from the time the Prophet ﷺ was in Mecca.

Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said in al-'Aridah: "The hadith of Jabir is authentic, and the verse in which is ﴿Over it are nineteen﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 30] is Meccan by consensus. How then would the Jews say this, when the Prophet was calling them to answer, and that took place in Medina? It is possible that the Companions said, 'We do not know,' because they had not read the verse, nor had it spread among them; that is, because they were from the Ansar, who had not received this verse from the surah al-Muddaththir, given the distance of the time of its revelation in Mecca; and those who used to gather with the Jews and whom the Jews questioned were the Ansar. He said: It is also possible that the Companions could not determine that the nineteen were the guardians unless Allah had specified it, until the Prophet ﷺ declared it." End of quotation. Thus the truth of His words, ﴿so that those who were given the Scripture may become certain﴾, became manifest years after the time of its revelation.

The meaning of ﴿and those who believe may increase in faith﴾ is that they believe in it along with what they believe of the unseen, so that a particular component increases in their minds within the particulars of the reality of their faith in the unseen. This is a quantitative increase, not a qualitative one, because the reality of faith is affirmation and conviction, and that does not admit of increase. By this same reasoning is to be interpreted everything that has come concerning the increase of faith in the statements of the Book and the Sunnah and in the statements of the pious predecessors of the Community.

His words, ﴿and those who were given the Scripture and the believers may not doubt﴾, are coordinated with ﴿so that those who were given the Scripture may become certain﴾, meaning: so that doubt may be removed from them, and no doubt may afflict them after knowledge, since it is certainty based on evidence. Even if the two groups differ in acting upon their knowledge, the believers knew and acted, while those who were given the Scripture knew and were obstinate, so their knowledge became a proof against them and a regret in their souls.

The purpose of mentioning this is to prepare for the mention of the obstinacy of those in whose hearts is a disease and of the disbelievers in their misunderstanding of this number, as a preparation by allusion before explicit statement; for when it is said, ﴿and those who were given the Scripture and the believers may not doubt﴾, those in whose hearts is a disease and the disbelievers feel that, since they have doubted this, they are below the rank of those who were given the Scripture, because they do not dispute that those who were given the Scripture are superior to them in intellect and sounder in speech. For this reason it is followed by ﴿and so that those in whose hearts is a disease and the disbelievers may say, "What did Allah intend by this as an example?"﴾, meaning: so that they may say this statement, expressing what is in their souls of disparagement of the Qur'an, without knowing the confirmation by those who were given the Scripture.

The lam is the lam of consequence, like that in His words, ﴿Then the family of Pharaoh picked him up, so that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8].

The disease in the hearts is ill intention toward the Qur'an and the Messenger ﷺ, and these are the ones who remained hesitating between becoming Muslims and remaining in polytheism, such as al-Akhnas ibn Shariq and al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah. The intended meaning of "those in whose hearts is a disease" is not the hypocrites, because the hypocrites did not appear except in Medina after the Hijrah, and this verse is Meccan.

"What did Allah intend" is an interrogative of denial, since (ma) is interrogative, and (dha) is originally a demonstrative noun; when it comes after the two interrogatives (ma) or (min), it conveys the meaning of "who" or "which" (alladhi). Its full sense is: What is the matter that Allah intended by this speech while it is an example? The meaning is: Allah did not intend this number that is exemplified. The negation of Allah's intention regarding the number is a metonymy for denying that Allah said that; the meaning is: Allah did not intend the number exemplified. So by negating Allah's intention for the description of this number they meant denying that this number agrees with reality, since they deny its benefit; in fact they intended to deny that this is a revelation from Allah.

The reference of "by this" is to His words, ﴿Over it are nineteen﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 30].

(Mathalan, "as an example") is in the accusative as a circumstantial state of (hadha, "this"). The mathal is the description: that is, by this number, which is nineteen; that is, what is the benefit of this number rather than another, such as twenty?

The mathal is the description of an astonishing condition, that is, what He described of the number of the guardians of the Fire, like His words, ﴿The likeness of the Garden which the righteous have been promised﴾ [Muhammad: 15], etc.

[Page 318]

A parallel to this was mentioned earlier at His words, ﴿As for those who disbelieve, they say, "What did Allah intend by this as an example?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26], in surah al-Baqarah.

* * *

﴿Thus Allah leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾. The demonstrative ("thus") refers to what the preceding speech contained, from His words, ﴿so that those who were given the Scripture may become certain﴾ up to His words, "as an example," by way of interpreting what the speech contained as what is mentioned: that is, like that misguidance that befalls those in whose hearts is a disease and the disbelievers, and that which befalls those who were given the Scripture after they became certain but did not believe, Allah leads astray whom He wills of His servants to be led astray; and like that guidance which the believers were guided to, so that it increased their faith along with their faith, Allah guides whom He wills.

The purpose of this comparison is to bring the intelligible meaning closer, namely that Allah the Exalted disposes by creating the causes of the states that befall humans, to a sensible meaning known in an actual situation, as instruction for the Muslims and as an alert to reflection on acquiring what benefits their souls.

Its point of resemblance (wajh al-shabah) is the causal role in the guidance of those who are guided and the misguidance of those who go astray, in that each of the compared and the compared-to is something God made a cause and willed for a wisdom that His knowledge required. Thus people vary in the extent of their understanding of it, between one who is guided and one who doubts, with varying degrees of doubt, and between one who is obstinate and a disbeliever, and one of poor understanding who is a disbeliever.

This expression is great in its scope regarding the differing ways in which minds receive the realities and benefit from them or the opposite, according to the variation of their faculties, their understandings, and the compositions of their natures, which proceed in a chain from correctness to its like, or from hesitation and disturbance to its like, or from rancor and stubbornness to its like. Thus the comparison in His words "Thus" (kadhalika) encompasses many states and forms that become manifest in external reality.

The attribution of misguidance to God, Exalted is He, is based on His being the originator of the primary causes in natures, the acquisition of desires, the interrelation of the conditions of the world with one another, the call of the prophets and righteous ones to good, and the resistance of the leaders of misguidance to those calls. These are the causes that led the astray to their misguidance and the guided to their guidance. And all of them are part of God's creation. So nothing remains for souls that desire good and salvation except to expose themselves to one of the two paths (al-mahi'atayn) after detachment and reflection: "It has what it earned and it bears what it has earned" [al-Baqarah: 286].

Page 319

God's will in this is the attachment of His knowledge to the conduct of the guided and the astray.

The position of "thus" (kadhalika) is in the accusative by substitution for the absolute object (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq), because the prepositional phrase here is an attribute of a deleted verbal noun (masdar) indicated by the attribute. The estimate is: God misguides whom He wills and guides whom He wills with misguidance and guidance, "thus" the misguidance and the guidance. This is not of the same category as His words, "And thus We have made you a middle nation" [al-Baqarah: 143].

He placed the description of the absolute object first for emphasis on this comparison, because of what it guides to in terms of detail upon reflection on it. And from placing it first arose the embellishment of collection (husn al-jam'), then division (al-taqsim), since its division came with His words, "God misguides whom He wills and guides whom He wills."

* * *

"And none knows the hosts of your Lord except Him" is a comprehensive statement refuting the baseless conjectures that the misguided and those with sick hearts make when hearing reports about the unseen world and matters of the Hereafter, such as what Abu Jahl said about the guardians of Hell. It encompasses that and more, so this sentence has the status of a concluding statement (tadhyil).

"Junud" is the plural of "jund," which is a term for a body of an army, and it is used here metaphorically for the creatures that God appointed to execute His command, because they resemble soldiers in carrying out the intended purpose.

The attribution of "Lord" (rabb) to the pronoun of the Prophet ﷺ is an attribution of honour and an allusion that among the functions of those hosts is that the victory of the Prophet ﷺ comes through some of them. The negation of knowledge here is a negation of detailed knowledge of their numbers, their attributes and their characteristics, by the indication of the context, for the knowledge of the number of the guardians of Hell has been granted to people by information from God, but they do not know what lies beyond that.

* * *

"And it is nothing but a reminder to mankind" has many meanings, the highest of which is that this is a continuation of His words, "And We have not made their number but as a trial for those who disbelieve" [al-Muddathir: 31], on the basis that it proceeds in the manner of the wise style (al-uslub al-hakim), meaning: what benefits you is that you know that the report about the guardians of the Fire, that they are nineteen, has as its purpose that it be a reminder

Page 320

to mankind, so that they remember the abode of punishment through describing some of its attributes, because mentioning an attribute helps increase the recollection of the one described. So the purpose of the Qur'an is reminder, but the misguided and those with sick hearts have taken it as idle play, mockery and contention, by asking about why they are nineteen and why they were not twenty, or hundreds, or thousands.

The pronoun in "hiya" (it) on this view refers back to their number.

It is permissible that the pronoun refers back to the preceding speech, and the feminine form of its pronoun is due to interpreting it as the narrative, the attribute, or the Qur'anic verses.

The meaning is similar to the meaning on the first possibility.

It may refer to "Saqar," and it is a "reminder" in terms of the warning by it and the mention of its terrors.

The restriction (al-qasr) is directed toward a deleted genitive construction indicated by the context, its estimate being: "and its mention or its description or the like."

The pronoun "hiya" may refer to "junud rabbika," and the meaning is the same, and the estimate is the same: that is, "and its mention, or the number of some of them."

Al-Zajjaj permitted that the pronoun refer to the fire of this world, meaning: it reminds people of the fire of the Hereafter. He intends that this is of the same kind as God's words, "Have you considered the fire that you kindle? Is it you who produced its tree, or are We the producer? We have made it a reminder" [al-Waqi'ah: 71-73]. In this there is the embellishment of ambiguity (husn al-istikhdam).

It was also said that the meaning is: "And their number is only a reminder to mankind, so that they know God's independence of helpers and soldiers, and so that they do not think nineteen is a small number against the multitude of the people of the Fire."

These meanings are carried by the verse because of the excellence of its placement in this position, and this is from the eloquence of the Qur'an's composition. Had it come directly after His words, "Burning to the human being" [al-Muddathir: 29], the pronoun in "And it is nothing but a reminder" would have been purely referring back to Saqar, and this is part of the inimitability of the Qur'an through the placement of its sentences, as in the tenth introduction among the introductions of this commentary.

Between the word "bashar" mentioned here and the word "bashar" mentioned earlier in His words, "Burning to the human being" [al-Muddathir: 29], there is complete paronomasia (al-tajnis al-tamm).

[Page 321]

﴿Kallā﴾ (كَلّا) is a particle of deterrence (radʿ) and refutation (ibtāl). It most often occurs after a statement by one speaker, or by a speaker and a listener, as in His saying, ﴿The companions of Moses said, "Indeed, we are overtaken." He said, "No! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me."﴾ (Ash-Shu'ara: 61). It thus conveys deterrence from what the preceding reported statement contained. From the same usage is His saying, ﴿No! We will record what he says.﴾ (Maryam: 79) in Surah Maryam. It may also be placed before the statement when the aim is to hasten the deterrence and to create anticipation for hearing what follows. Here it is possible that it is a refutation of what precedes it, namely their saying, "So if Allah intends by this an example..." In that case, what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (i'tirāḍ), and His saying, ﴿By the moon﴾, begins a new statement, so pausing on ﴿kallā﴾ is good.

It is also possible that it is a particle of refutation placed before the statement that follows it, from His saying, ﴿Indeed, it is one of the greatest [matters]﴾ (al-Muddaththir: 35) and ﴿a warning to humanity﴾ (al-Muddaththir: 36). This is placed first for emphasis, to refute what follows of the content of His saying, ﴿a warning to humanity﴾, meaning: it is their due that they be warned by it, but most of them did not heed the warning, in the manner of the meaning of His saying, ﴿And how will the reminder be for him?﴾ (al-Fajr: 23). In that case it is good to connect it in recitation to what follows it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 74, verses 35–37:

﴿By the moon﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 32] ﴿and by the night when it turns its back﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 33] ﴿and by the morning when it brightens﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 34] ﴿Indeed, it is one of the greatest (calamities)﴾ ﴿a warning to mankind﴾ ﴿to whoever among you wills to go forward or to lag behind﴾.

The wa (و) with which this sentence begins is the wa of oath (qasam, an oath). This oath may serve as a concluding statement (tadhyil, an appended closing phrase) that confirms what precedes it, confirming the denial and refutation implied by (kalla, "no indeed"), concerning their claim about the number of the guardians of Hell. In that case the sentence (﴿Indeed, it is one of the greatest﴾) is a justification (ta'lil) for the denial that (kalla) conveys, and the pronoun in (innaha, "indeed it") refers to (Saqar, Hell). That is, it is worthy that one be reminded by it, and therefore whoever does not take heed from it deserves to be rebuked and restrained.

On this interpretation, the oath clause is parenthetical (mu'taridah) between the statement and its justification. It is also possible that the oath is the opening of the speech that follows, and the sentence (﴿Indeed, it is one of the greatest﴾) is the answer to the oath, with the pronoun referring to (Saqar). That is, Saqar is among the greatest of terrors. In this case the pronoun (innaha) does not admit all the possibilities that applied to the pronoun in (﴿and it is not but a reminder﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31]).

These are three oaths, for the sake of added emphasis, since when verbal emphasis is achieved by repetition, it is generally repeated three times. He swore by a great created thing, and by two great states that are among the signs of God Most High's power.

The rationale for swearing by the moon, by the night when it turns its back, and by the morning when it brightens is that these three are the things by which lights appear amid darkness. Therefore they suit the two states of guidance and misguidance mentioned in His words (﴿Thus God leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31]) and in His words (﴿and it is not but a reminder for mankind﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31]). Thus in this oath there is an allusion to portraying the condition of the two groups of people at the descent of the Qur'an, by the image of light piercing through darkness.

The turning back of the night (idbar al-layl) means the approach of its passing at dawn, and the brightening of the morning (isfar al-subh) means the beginning of the appearance of the light of dawn.

Each of (idh, "when") and (idha, "when") is a noun of time, placed in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "the night" and "the morning." That is, He swears by it in this wondrous state, which indicates the firm and harmonious order by which God erases the darkness of disbelief with the light of Islam. God Most High said (﴿A Book which We have sent down to you that you may bring mankind out of darknesses into light﴾ [Ibrahim: 1]).

The sentence (﴿Indeed, it is one of the greatest﴾) has been treated as a proverb (mathal).

The meaning of (ihda, "one of") is that it is the singular, distinguished one among the greatest in magnitude, having no equal. It is like saying: "He is one of the men," not meaning that he is one of them, but meaning that he is singularly prominent among them, outstanding and conspicuous, as was explained earlier in His words (﴿Leave Me with the one whom I created alone﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 11]). And in the proverb: "This is one of Luqman's little gifts" (huzaiyat).

Nafi', Hamzah, Hafs, Ya'qub and Khalaf read (idh adbar) with a sukun on the dhal of (idh) and a fatha on the hamza of (adbar) with a sukun on its dal. He swears by the night in its state of turning its back, which has passed, and which is a renewed state that passes, arrives and is anticipated. Whatever time one considers together with it, it is worthy that He swear by its occurrence in it. For this reason He swore by the morning when it brightens together with the noun of the future tense. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, al-Kisa'i and Abu Ja'far read (idha dabara) with a fatha on the dotted dhal of (idha), followed by an alif, and a fatha on the undotted dal of (dabara), as a bare past-tense verb. It is said: "dabara" with the meaning of "adbara" (to turn back). From this is its description as al-dabir in their saying: "amsi al-dabir" (yesterday, the past). Just as it is said "qabala" with the meaning of "aqbala" (to come forward). Accordingly the oath is by the future state of the night's turning back after the revelation of the verse, in the pattern of (﴿when it brightens﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 34]) in the reading of all. All of this is sound, and in the reading of Nafi' and those who agree with him there is a variety (tafannun) in the oath.

Al-kubar (the greatest) is the plural of al-kubra (the greatest) within its category. They formed this plural in a manner not following the usual pattern of its class, because the form fu'la should be pluralized in the sound feminine plural as kubrayat. As for the pattern fu'al, it is a broken plural of fu'la, as in ghurfa and ghuraf (room, rooms). However, they treated the feminine with the alif as analogous to the feminine with the ha', because they interpreted it as a name for a great calamity, and did not consider it as the quality described as greatness, i.e., the feminine of "the greatest." Therefore they made the feminine alif in it function like the feminine ha', and pluralized it like the feminine with the ha' of the form fu'la. They did not do that with its counterparts, such as 'uzma (greatest).

The word (nadhiran, "a warning") is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) from the pronoun in (innaha). That is, indeed it is the greatest of the great things while warning mankind, and it suffices as a warner.

Nadhir (warner) means one who warns. Its origin is a description by a verbal noun (masdar), because (nadhiran) came in the verbal nouns just as (nakir, denial) came. When a verbal noun is used as a description or as a predicate, it requires the singular and masculine form. The description by "nadhir" became so common that it became like a proper noun for the one who warns.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 74, verses 35–37:

﴿By the moon﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 32] ﴿and by the night when it turns its back﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 33] ﴿and by the morning when it brightens﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 34] ﴿Indeed, it is one of the greatest (calamities)﴾ ﴿a warning to mankind﴾ ﴿to whoever among you wills to go forward or to lag behind﴾.

The wa (و) with which this sentence begins is the wa of oath (qasam, an oath). This oath may serve as a concluding statement (tadhyil, an appended closing phrase) that confirms what precedes it, confirming the denial and refutation implied by (kalla, "no indeed"), concerning their claim about the number of the guardians of Hell. In that case the sentence (﴿Indeed, it is one of the greatest﴾) is a justification (ta'lil) for the denial that (kalla) conveys, and the pronoun in (innaha, "indeed it") refers to (Saqar, Hell). That is, it is worthy that one be reminded by it, and therefore whoever does not take heed from it deserves to be rebuked and restrained.

On this interpretation, the oath clause is parenthetical (mu'taridah) between the statement and its justification. It is also possible that the oath is the opening of the speech that follows, and the sentence (﴿Indeed, it is one of the greatest﴾) is the answer to the oath, with the pronoun referring to (Saqar). That is, Saqar is among the greatest of terrors. In this case the pronoun (innaha) does not admit all the possibilities that applied to the pronoun in (﴿and it is not but a reminder﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31]).

These are three oaths, for the sake of added emphasis, since when verbal emphasis is achieved by repetition, it is generally repeated three times. He swore by a great created thing, and by two great states that are among the signs of God Most High's power.

The rationale for swearing by the moon, by the night when it turns its back, and by the morning when it brightens is that these three are the things by which lights appear amid darkness. Therefore they suit the two states of guidance and misguidance mentioned in His words (﴿Thus God leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31]) and in His words (﴿and it is not but a reminder for mankind﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31]). Thus in this oath there is an allusion to portraying the condition of the two groups of people at the descent of the Qur'an, by the image of light piercing through darkness.

The turning back of the night (idbar al-layl) means the approach of its passing at dawn, and the brightening of the morning (isfar al-subh) means the beginning of the appearance of the light of dawn.

Each of (idh, "when") and (idha, "when") is a noun of time, placed in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "the night" and "the morning." That is, He swears by it in this wondrous state, which indicates the firm and harmonious order by which God erases the darkness of disbelief with the light of Islam. God Most High said (﴿A Book which We have sent down to you that you may bring mankind out of darknesses into light﴾ [Ibrahim: 1]).

The sentence (﴿Indeed, it is one of the greatest﴾) has been treated as a proverb (mathal).

The meaning of (ihda, "one of") is that it is the singular, distinguished one among the greatest in magnitude, having no equal. It is like saying: "He is one of the men," not meaning that he is one of them, but meaning that he is singularly prominent among them, outstanding and conspicuous, as was explained earlier in His words (﴿Leave Me with the one whom I created alone﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 11]). And in the proverb: "This is one of Luqman's little gifts" (huzaiyat).

Nafi', Hamzah, Hafs, Ya'qub and Khalaf read (idh adbar) with a sukun on the dhal of (idh) and a fatha on the hamza of (adbar) with a sukun on its dal. He swears by the night in its state of turning its back, which has passed, and which is a renewed state that passes, arrives and is anticipated. Whatever time one considers together with it, it is worthy that He swear by its occurrence in it. For this reason He swore by the morning when it brightens together with the noun of the future tense. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, al-Kisa'i and Abu Ja'far read (idha dabara) with a fatha on the dotted dhal of (idha), followed by an alif, and a fatha on the undotted dal of (dabara), as a bare past-tense verb. It is said: "dabara" with the meaning of "adbara" (to turn back). From this is its description as al-dabir in their saying: "amsi al-dabir" (yesterday, the past). Just as it is said "qabala" with the meaning of "aqbala" (to come forward). Accordingly the oath is by the future state of the night's turning back after the revelation of the verse, in the pattern of (﴿when it brightens﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 34]) in the reading of all. All of this is sound, and in the reading of Nafi' and those who agree with him there is a variety (tafannun) in the oath.

As for the pattern fu'al, it is a broken plural of fu'la, as in ghurfa and ghuraf (room, rooms). They did not do that with its counterparts, such as 'uzma (greatest).

**[Page 325]**

This is a resumptive explanatory clause (*istinaf bayani*, a clause that answers an implied question for the listener), explaining the outcome of the choice mentioned in His words ﴿for whoever among you wills to go forward or to lag behind﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 37]. That is: every soul is held in pledge (*rahina*) by what it has earned, whether of advancing or lagging behind or otherwise. It is therefore perceptive of its own self, so that it may earn what leads it to bliss or to the Blazing Fire.

*Rahina* (رَهِينَةٌ) is a predicate of "every soul," and it means *marhuna* (held in pledge).

*Al-rahn* (the pledge) means bonds and confinement, and from it comes *al-rahn* in debt. It may also be used for constancy and attachment, as in *faras rihan* (two horses in a race). Both meanings are valid here, according to the difference in circumstance. A pledge is only taken to secure a claim against the risk that the debtor might escape it, so *al-rahn* implies firmness in holding. From this comes the sense of hostages of war, whom the stronger party among the defeated people takes as a guarantee lest the people break the terms of the peace, and until they pay the blood-money for the slain, so that retaliation is exacted from the hostages.

On this basis, His words "every soul" are intended to mean specifically the souls of those who were warned among mankind. It is then a general term intended in a particular sense by context, namely the context of what the root *rahina* conveys of confinement and captivity.

The *ba'* (ب) in *bima kasabat* denotes accompaniment, not causation.

The apparent meaning is that this is a statement of general justice, and not specifically a threat to the people of evil.

*Rahina* is a verbal noun (*masdar*) of the form *fa'ila(tun)*, like *shatima(tun)*. It is one of the verbal nouns associated with a *ha'* like the feminine *ha'*, such as *al-fu'ula(tun)* and *al-fa''ala(tun)*. It is not of the pattern *fa'il*, which is an adjective in the sense of the passive participle, like *qatila(tun)*. Had it been intended as an adjective, it would have been said *rahin*, because *fa'il* in the sense of *maf'ul* is used without distinction between masculine and feminine when it agrees with its noun, as it does here. The predication by a verbal noun is for emphasis, following the manner of the verse of Musawwar ibn Ziyada al-Harithi:

*Abd al-ladhi bil-na'fi na'fi Kuwaykibin*
*rahinata ramsin dhi turabin wa jandali*

Do you not see that he kept the *ha'* in the adjective of the masculine? Otherwise it would not have required the feminine.

The exception in His words ﴿except the companions of the right hand﴾ is a disjunctive exception (*istithna' munqati'*, an exception not of the same category as what precedes it).

The companions of the right hand are the people of good. Their marks at the Gathering are by the directions of the right hand, in the receiving of the records and at the place of reckoning and otherwise. The right hand is the direction of the people of honour in reckoning, like the direction of the right of the Throne, or the right of the place of holiness on the Day of Gathering, which our description cannot encompass. The mark of the people of evil is the left, in the receiving of their records of deeds, at their stations, and otherwise.

His words ﴿in gardens﴾ may be connected to His words ﴿they will ask one another﴾, placed first for emphasis. ﴿They will ask one another﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from ﴿the companions of the right hand﴾, and it is the basis of the detail for which the disjunctive exception was brought.

It may also be that ﴿in gardens﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, whose estimate is: "they are in gardens." The clause is then a resumptive explanatory clause for the content of the exceptive clause, and ﴿they will ask one another﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the omitted pronoun.

The meaning of ﴿they will ask one another﴾ may be on the apparent form of the reciprocal pattern, indicating the action coming from two sides. That is: the companions of the right hand ask one another about the state of the guilty. Then the clause ﴿What brought you into Saqar?﴾ is an explanation of the clause ﴿they will ask one another﴾. The pronoun of address in *salakakum* (you) implies an omitted element. The estimate is: "so they will ask the guilty, 'What brought you into Saqar?'" This is not a shift in person. Or one of those questioned says to his companions, in answer to those who question them: "We said to them: 'What brought you into Saqar?'"

It may also be that the reciprocal form is used in the sense of repetition of the action, that is: the questioning of each one of them is frequent and repeated, or it is from the enumeration of the questioning for the sake of the enumeration of the questioners.

Al-Zamakhshari said, in his commentary on His words ﴿Fear God, by whom you ask one another﴾ [al-Nisa': 1] at the beginning of Surat al-Nisa': "It is like your saying *tada'ayna* (we called one another)." It is also transmitted from him that he said here: "If the speaker is singular, one says *da'awtu* (I called); if the speaker is plural, one says *tada'ayna* (we called one another). Its parallel is *ramaytuhu* (I shot it) and *taramaynahu* (we shot it at one another), and *ra'aytu al-hilal* (I saw the crescent) and *ta'ra'aynahu* (we saw it together); and this is not a reciprocal action from two sides." This is what the author of *al-Kashshaf* mentioned in the Surat al-Nisa'. That is, it is an action from one side with a large number of agents. On this basis, the object of *yatasa'aluna* (they ask one another) is omitted, indicated by His words ﴿about the guilty﴾.

The estimate is: "they ask the guilty about them," that is, about the cause of their being in Saqar. This is indicated by the explanation of the clause *yatasa'aluna* by the clause ﴿What brought you into Saqar?﴾, for ﴿What brought you into Saqar?﴾ explains the questioning.

The root meaning of *salaka* (to thread) is to insert something between the parts of a thing, literally, and from it comes *silk al-iqd* (the string of a necklace). It is used here metaphorically for driving them in. His words ﴿Thus We let it enter into the hearts of the guilty﴾ [al-Hijr: 12] were mentioned in Surat al-Hijr, and His words ﴿He will make him enter a severe torment﴾ [al-Jinn: 17] in Surat al-Jinn. The meaning is: "What drove you into Saqar?"

If the question is in its literal sense and the interrogation is used in its original meaning, then the motive for the question is either forgetting what they had known in the world of the causes of reward and punishment. In that case the generality of *yatasa'aluna*, referring to the companions of the right hand, and the generality of *al-mujrimin* (the guilty) remain as they apparently are. Each of the companions of the right hand looks down on the guilty from the heights of Paradise and asks them about the cause of their entering the Fire, and the answer comes. This is an inspiration from God, so that the people of Paradise may praise Him for what they took up of the causes of their deliverance from what befell the guilty, and rejoice in that.

Or it is a question directed by some of the companions of the right hand to people whom they had supposed to be among the people of Paradise, but whom they saw in the Fire, being hypocrites or apostates after the death of their companions. Then the meaning of the companions of the right hand is some of them, and of the guilty some of them. This is like His words ﴿And some of them will turn to others, asking one another﴾ [al-Saffat: 27] ﴿They will say: 'You used to come to us from the right'﴾ [al-Saffat: 28], and the verses in Surat al-Saffat. And His words in it ﴿A speaker among them will say: "I had a companion"﴾ [al-Saffat: 51] ﴿saying: "Are you indeed among those who affirm?"﴾ [al-Saffat: 52] up to His words ﴿in the midst of the Blazing Fire﴾ [al-Saffat: 55].

If the question is not in its literal sense, and the interrogation is used to reproach or to rebuke, then the generality of the companions of the right hand and the generality of the guilty remain in their literal sense.

The guilty answered by mentioning the causes of their being thrown into the Fire, for they had understood only the apparent meaning of the interrogation. They mentioned four causes, which are the roots of sins, and they are: that they were not among the people of prayer, and so they deprived themselves of drawing near to God.

And that they were not among those who fed the needy, and that is transgression against the weak among people by withholding their right in wealth.

And that they used to engage in their customary vain talk, which did not go beyond supporting polytheism and harming the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers.

And that they denied the recompense, and so they did not seek what would save them. This is a metonymy for their not believing. They took the path of elaboration (*itnab*), suited to the situation of grief and anguish over what has passed. It is as if they said: "We were not among the believers," because the people of faith were known for being people of prayer, for giving a known right in their wealth to the beggar and the deprived, and for believing in the Hereafter and the Day of Recompense and affirming the messengers. All of this is gathered in His words in Surat al-Baqarah ﴿A guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2] ﴿who establish prayer and spend of what We have provided them﴾ [al-Anfal: 3] ﴿and who believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you, and in the Hereafter they are certain﴾ [al-Baqarah: 4].

The root meaning of *al-khawd* (plunging) is entering into water. It is often used metaphorically for repeated conversation, and its use in the Qur'an for argument and obstinacy that is not praiseworthy is well known. It is used here metaphorically for driving them in. His words ﴿Thus We let it enter into the hearts of the guilty﴾ [al-Hijr: 12] were mentioned in Surat al-Hijr, and His words ﴿He will make him enter a severe torment﴾ [al-Jinn: 17] in Surat al-Jinn. The meaning is: "What drove you into Saqar?"

If the question is in its literal sense and the interrogation is used in its original meaning, then the motive for the question is either forgetting what they had known in the world of the causes of reward and punishment. In that case the generality of *yatasa'aluna*, referring to the companions of the right hand, and the generality of *al-mujrimin* (the guilty) remain as they apparently are. Each of the companions of the right hand looks down on the guilty from the heights of Paradise and asks them about the cause of their entering the Fire, and the answer comes. This is an inspiration from God, so that the people of Paradise may praise Him for what they took up of the causes of their deliverance from what befell the guilty, and rejoice in that.

Or it is a question directed by some of the companions of the right hand to people whom they had supposed to be among the people of Paradise, but whom they saw in the Fire, being hypocrites or apostates after the death of their companions. Then the meaning of the companions of the right hand is some of them, and of the guilty some of them. If the question is not in its literal sense, and the interrogation is used to reproach or to rebuke, then the generality of the companions of the right hand and the generality of the guilty remain in their literal sense.

The guilty answered by mentioning the causes of their being thrown into the Fire, for they had understood only the apparent meaning of the interrogation. They mentioned four causes, which are the roots of sins, and they are: that they were not among the people of prayer, and so they deprived themselves of drawing near to God.

And that they were not among those who fed the needy, and that is transgression against the weak among people by withholding their right in wealth.

And that they used to engage in their customary vain talk, which did not go beyond supporting polytheism and harming the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers.

And that they denied the recompense, and so they did not seek what would save them. This is a metonymy for their not believing. They took the path of elaboration (*itnab*), suited to the situation of grief and anguish over what has passed. It is as if they said: "We were not among the believers," because the people of faith were known for being people of prayer, for giving a known right in their wealth to the beggar and the deprived, and for believing in the Hereafter and the Day of Recompense and affirming the messengers. All of this is gathered in His words in Surat al-Baqarah ﴿A guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2] ﴿who establish prayer and spend of what We have provided them﴾ [al-Anfal: 3] ﴿and who believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you, and in the Hereafter they are certain﴾ [al-Baqarah: 4].

The root meaning of *al-khawd* (plunging) is entering into water. It is often used metaphorically for repeated conversation, and its use in the Qur'an for argument and obstinacy that is not praiseworthy is well known. God said ﴿Leave them in their plunging, playing﴾ [al-An'am: 91], and other places. Taking the four causes in their answer together, along with the meaning of metonymy, there is nothing in the verse that supports those who say that unbelievers are addressed by the branches of the Law.

*Yawm al-Din* is the Day of Recompense and of reward.

*Al-yaqin* (certainty) is a verbal noun of *yaqina* (to know), like *fariha*, when one knows with knowledge in which there is no doubt and no hesitation. Its coming is used metaphorically for its occurrence after its absence, the occurrence after non-existence being likened to coming after departure.

The meaning is: "until we came to know that what we used to deny is真 established." In this sense, His words ﴿until certainty came to us﴾ are a limit (*ghaya*) for the clause ﴿we used to deny the Day of Recompense﴾.

*Al-yaqin* is also used for death, since its occurrence is known to every living being. So it may be intended here, as in His words ﴿And worship your Lord until certainty comes to you﴾ [al-Hijr: 99]. Then the clause ﴿until certainty came to us﴾ is a limit for the four preceding clauses from His words ﴿we were not among those who prayed﴾ up to ﴿the Day of Recompense﴾.

The meaning is: "We did these things throughout the whole of our lives."

The present-tense verbs in His words ﴿we were not, we used to feed not, we used to plunge, we used to deny﴾ indicate that this was their habit and continued in them throughout their lives.

The verse contains an indication that the Muslim who neglected to establish prayer and to give *zakat* deserves a share of Saqar in proportion to his neglect, and according to what God wills of the balancing of his good and evil deeds, his outward and inward conduct, and whether before intercession or after it.

God has deprived these guilty unbelievers of intercession being of benefit to them, so perhaps intercession will benefit believers according to their degrees.

In His words ﴿So the intercession of the interceders will not benefit them﴾ there is an allusion to the establishment of intercession for others on the Day of Resurrection in general, and its details are in the authentic reports.

The Arabic word *al-tafa'ul* and similar pattern terms were rendered descriptively. One sentence in the middle of the text (the one ending in "true") contained an Arabic word that I have rendered as "真 established"; the intended meaning is "established."

**[Page 325]**

This is a resumptive explanatory clause (*istinaf bayani*, a clause that answers an implied question for the listener), explaining the outcome of the choice mentioned in His words ﴿for whoever among you wills to go forward or to lag behind﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 37]. That is: every soul is held in pledge (*rahina*) by what it has earned, whether of advancing or lagging behind or otherwise. It is therefore perceptive of its own self, so that it may earn what leads it to bliss or to the Blazing Fire.

*Rahina* (رَهِينَةٌ) is a predicate of "every soul," and it means *marhuna* (held in pledge).

*Al-rahn* (the pledge) means bonds and confinement, and from it comes *al-rahn* in debt. It may also be used for constancy and attachment, as in *faras rihan* (two horses in a race). Both meanings are valid here, according to the difference in circumstance. A pledge is only taken to secure a claim against the risk that the debtor might escape it, so *al-rahn* implies firmness in holding. From this comes the sense of hostages of war, whom the stronger party among the defeated people takes as a guarantee lest the people break the terms of the peace, and until they pay the blood-money for the slain, so that retaliation is exacted from the hostages.

On this basis, His words "every soul" are intended to mean specifically the souls of those who were warned among mankind. It is then a general term intended in a particular sense by context, namely the context of what the root *rahina* conveys of confinement and captivity.

The *ba'* (ب) in *bima kasabat* denotes accompaniment, not causation.

The apparent meaning is that this is a statement of general justice, and not specifically a threat to the people of evil.

*Rahina* is a verbal noun (*masdar*) of the form *fa'ila(tun)*, like *shatima(tun)*. It is one of the verbal nouns associated with a *ha'* like the feminine *ha'*, such as *al-fu'ula(tun)* and *al-fa''ala(tun)*. It is not of the pattern *fa'il*, which is an adjective in the sense of the passive participle, like *qatila(tun)*. Had it been intended as an adjective, it would have been said *rahin*, because *fa'il* in the sense of *maf'ul* is used without distinction between masculine and feminine when it agrees with its noun, as it does here. The predication by a verbal noun is for emphasis, following the manner of the verse of Musawwar ibn Ziyada al-Harithi:

*Abd al-ladhi bil-na'fi na'fi Kuwaykibin*
*rahinata ramsin dhi turabin wa jandali*

Do you not see that he kept the *ha'* in the adjective of the masculine? Otherwise it would not have required the feminine.

The exception in His words ﴿except the companions of the right hand﴾ is a disjunctive exception (*istithna' munqati'*, an exception not of the same category as what precedes it).

The companions of the right hand are the people of good. Their marks at the Gathering are by the directions of the right hand, in the receiving of the records and at the place of reckoning and otherwise. The right hand is the direction of the people of honour in reckoning, like the direction of the right of the Throne, or the right of the place of holiness on the Day of Gathering, which our description cannot encompass. The mark of the people of evil is the left, in the receiving of their records of deeds, at their stations, and otherwise.

His words ﴿in gardens﴾ may be connected to His words ﴿they will ask one another﴾, placed first for emphasis. ﴿They will ask one another﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from ﴿the companions of the right hand﴾, and it is the basis of the detail for which the disjunctive exception was brought.

It may also be that ﴿in gardens﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, whose estimate is: "they are in gardens." The clause is then a resumptive explanatory clause for the content of the exceptive clause, and ﴿they will ask one another﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the omitted pronoun.

The meaning of ﴿they will ask one another﴾ may be on the apparent form of the reciprocal pattern, indicating the action coming from two sides. That is: the companions of the right hand ask one another about the state of the guilty. Then the clause ﴿What brought you into Saqar?﴾ is an explanation of the clause ﴿they will ask one another﴾. The pronoun of address in *salakakum* (you) implies an omitted element. The estimate is: "so they will ask the guilty, 'What brought you into Saqar?'" This is not a shift in person. Or one of those questioned says to his companions, in answer to those who question them: "We said to them: 'What brought you into Saqar?'"

It may also be that the reciprocal form is used in the sense of repetition of the action, that is: the questioning of each one of them is frequent and repeated, or it is from the enumeration of the questioning for the sake of the enumeration of the questioners.

Al-Zamakhshari said, in his commentary on His words ﴿Fear God, by whom you ask one another﴾ [al-Nisa': 1] at the beginning of Surat al-Nisa': "It is like your saying *tada'ayna* (we called one another)." It is also transmitted from him that he said here: "If the speaker is singular, one says *da'awtu* (I called); if the speaker is plural, one says *tada'ayna* (we called one another). Its parallel is *ramaytuhu* (I shot it) and *taramaynahu* (we shot it at one another), and *ra'aytu al-hilal* (I saw the crescent) and *ta'ra'aynahu* (we saw it together); and this is not a reciprocal action from two sides." This is what the author of *al-Kashshaf* mentioned in the Surat al-Nisa'. That is, it is an action from one side with a large number of agents. On this basis, the object of *yatasa'aluna* (they ask one another) is omitted, indicated by His words ﴿about the guilty﴾.

The estimate is: "they ask the guilty about them," that is, about the cause of their being in Saqar. This is indicated by the explanation of the clause *yatasa'aluna* by the clause ﴿What brought you into Saqar?﴾, for ﴿What brought you into Saqar?﴾ explains the questioning.

The root meaning of *salaka* (to thread) is to insert something between the parts of a thing, literally, and from it comes *silk al-iqd* (the string of a necklace). It is used here metaphorically for driving them in. His words ﴿Thus We let it enter into the hearts of the guilty﴾ [al-Hijr: 12] were mentioned in Surat al-Hijr, and His words ﴿He will make him enter a severe torment﴾ [al-Jinn: 17] in Surat al-Jinn. The meaning is: "What drove you into Saqar?"

If the question is in its literal sense and the interrogation is used in its original meaning, then the motive for the question is either forgetting what they had known in the world of the causes of reward and punishment. In that case the generality of *yatasa'aluna*, referring to the companions of the right hand, and the generality of *al-mujrimin* (the guilty) remain as they apparently are. Each of the companions of the right hand looks down on the guilty from the heights of Paradise and asks them about the cause of their entering the Fire, and the answer comes. This is an inspiration from God, so that the people of Paradise may praise Him for what they took up of the causes of their deliverance from what befell the guilty, and rejoice in that.

Or it is a question directed by some of the companions of the right hand to people whom they had supposed to be among the people of Paradise, but whom they saw in the Fire, being hypocrites or apostates after the death of their companions. Then the meaning of the companions of the right hand is some of them, and of the guilty some of them. This is like His words ﴿And some of them will turn to others, asking one another﴾ [al-Saffat: 27] ﴿They will say: 'You used to come to us from the right'﴾ [al-Saffat: 28], and the verses in Surat al-Saffat. And His words in it ﴿A speaker among them will say: "I had a companion"﴾ [al-Saffat: 51] ﴿saying: "Are you indeed among those who affirm?"﴾ [al-Saffat: 52] up to His words ﴿in the midst of the Blazing Fire﴾ [al-Saffat: 55].

If the question is not in its literal sense, and the interrogation is used to reproach or to rebuke, then the generality of the companions of the right hand and the generality of the guilty remain in their literal sense.

The guilty answered by mentioning the causes of their being thrown into the Fire, for they had understood only the apparent meaning of the interrogation. They mentioned four causes, which are the roots of sins, and they are: that they were not among the people of prayer, and so they deprived themselves of drawing near to God.

And that they were not among those who fed the needy, and that is transgression against the weak among people by withholding their right in wealth.

And that they used to engage in their customary vain talk, which did not go beyond supporting polytheism and harming the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers.

And that they denied the recompense, and so they did not seek what would save them. This is a metonymy for their not believing. They took the path of elaboration (*itnab*), suited to the situation of grief and anguish over what has passed. It is as if they said: "We were not among the believers," because the people of faith were known for being people of prayer, for giving a known right in their wealth to the beggar and the deprived, and for believing in the Hereafter and the Day of Recompense and affirming the messengers. All of this is gathered in His words in Surat al-Baqarah ﴿A guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2] ﴿who establish prayer and spend of what We have provided them﴾ [al-Anfal: 3] ﴿and who believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you, and in the Hereafter they are certain﴾ [al-Baqarah: 4].

The root meaning of *al-khawd* (plunging) is entering into water. It is often used metaphorically for repeated conversation, and its use in the Qur'an for argument and obstinacy that is not praiseworthy is well known. God said ﴿Leave them in their plunging, playing﴾ [al-An'am: 91], and other places. His words ﴿When you see those who engage in plunging into Our signs, turn away from them until they plunge into some other discourse﴾ [al-An'am: 68] combine both usages.

Taking the four causes in their answer together, along with the meaning of metonymy, there is nothing in the verse that supports those who say that unbelievers are addressed by the branches of the Law.

*Yawm al-Din* is the Day of Recompense and of reward.

*Al-yaqin* (certainty) is a verbal noun of *yaqina* (to know), like *fariha*, when one knows with knowledge in which there is no doubt and no hesitation. Its coming is used metaphorically for its occurrence after its absence, the occurrence after non-existence being likened to coming after departure.

The meaning is: "until we came to know that what we used to deny is真 established." In this sense, His words ﴿until certainty came to us﴾ are a limit (*ghaya*) for the clause ﴿we used to deny the Day of Recompense﴾.

*Al-yaqin* is also used for death, since its occurrence is known to every living being. So it may be intended here, as in His words ﴿And worship your Lord until certainty comes to you﴾ [al-Hijr: 99]. Then the clause ﴿until certainty came to us﴾ is a limit for the four preceding clauses from His words ﴿we were not among those who prayed﴾ up to ﴿the Day of Recompense﴾.

The meaning is: "We did these things throughout the whole of our lives."

The present-tense verbs in His words ﴿we were not, we used to feed not, we used to plunge, we used to deny﴾ indicate that this was their habit and continued in them throughout their lives.

The verse contains an indication that the Muslim who neglected to establish prayer and to give *zakat* deserves a share of Saqar in proportion to his neglect, and according to what God wills of the balancing of his good and evil deeds, his outward and inward conduct, and whether before intercession or after it.

God has deprived these guilty unbelievers of intercession being of benefit to them, so perhaps intercession will benefit believers according to their degrees.

In His words ﴿So the intercession of the interceders will not benefit them﴾ there is an allusion to the establishment of intercession for others on the Day of Resurrection in general, and its details are in the authentic reports.

The *fa'* (ف) in ﴿So the intercession of the interceders will not benefit them﴾ is a consequence of His words ﴿every soul is held in pledge by what it has earned﴾. That is: they remain perpetually held in pledge in Saqar.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 74, verses 49–51:

Page 329

﴿So what is wrong with them that they turn away from the reminder?﴾ ﴿As if they were startled donkeys﴾ ﴿fleeing from a lion﴾. (1) This is a consequence (tafri') expressing wonder at their insistence on turning away from that which is a reminder, following His words (﴿And it is not but a reminder to mankind﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31]).

The phrase "the reminder" (al-tadhkira) is stated as a noun explicitly rather than with a pronoun, as in saying "turning away from it," so that the denial and wonder are not restricted to their turning away from the reminder of warning about Saqar. Rather, the intent is generalization: their turning away from every reminder, the greatest of which is the reminder of the Qur'an, as is appropriate to the context of turning away. God the Exalted says (﴿It is not but a reminder to the worlds﴾ [Yusuf: 104]).

"Ma lahum" is an interrogative used to express wonder at the strangeness of their state, to such an extent that it is fitting for questioners to ask about it. It is a metonymic figure (majaz mursal) through the relation of necessary association (mulazama). "Lahum" is the predicate of "ma," the interrogative. The implied sense is: "What is established for them?" "Mu'ridin" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "lahum," meaning: one asks about them in this strange state.

The construction "ma laka" and similar expressions may be accompanied by a circumstantial element attached to its pronoun, either a single word or a clause, as in "ma laka la ta'manna 'alayya Yusuf" in Surat Yusuf, and the Almighty's words (﴿So what is wrong with them that they do not believe?﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 20]) in Surat al-Inshiqaq, and His words (﴿What is wrong with you? How do you judge?﴾ [al-Qalam: 36]) in Surat al-Saffat and Surat al-Qalam. "'An al-tadhkira" is attached to "mu'ridin."

Their imagined state of turning away is likened to the state of wild donkeys that flee from what startles them.

"Al-humur" is the plural of "himar," which is the wild ass. It is very skittish when it senses the sound of the hunter, and this is an instance of likening an intelligible matter to a sensible one.

The description of skittishness, swift movement and fleeing has frequently been applied to wild beasts, whether wild donkeys or wild cattle, when they sense what they fear, as Labid said in likening his riding-camel's swiftness to a wild animal pursued by the hunter:

So she sensed the sound of the human and it startled her, from a distant place, while the human was her illness.

This is frequent in Arab poetry in the Jahiliyya and Islam, as in the Mu'allaqa of Tarafa, the Mu'allaqa of Labid, the Mu'allaqa of al-Harith, and in the rajaz verses of al-Hajjaj and his son Ru'ba, and in the poetry of Dhu al-Rumma.

Page 330

The sin and the ta' in "mustanfira" serve to intensify the description, like: istakmala, istajaba, is'ajaba, istaskhara, istakhraja, istanbata, meaning: fleeing with strong flight, so that it runs at the utmost speed of running.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far read "mustanfaratun" with a fatha on the fa', meaning that a fleer caused it to flee, i.e. made it flee; it is from istanfarahu, the transitive form meaning anfarahu. The passive construction indicates the general first and then the detail with His words (﴿it flees from a lion﴾).

The majority read it with a kasra on the fa', meaning that they themselves fled, like istajaba, so the clause "farrat min qaswara" is an explanation of the cause of their fleeing.

In Tafsir al-Razi, from Abu 'Ali al-Farisi: Muhammad ibn Sallam said: "I asked Abu Sawwar al-Ghanawi, who was an eloquent Bedouin, and I said: 'Kaannahum humur madha?' ('As if they were donkeys of what?'). He said: 'Mustanfara,' with a fatha on the fa'. I said to him: 'Rather, it is: farrat min qaswara.' He said: 'Did they flee?' I said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Then it is mustanfira,' and he kasra'd the fa'."

As for "qaswara": it is said to be a collective noun (ism jam') of qaswar, which is the archer, or it is a plural against analogy, since the pattern fa'lala does not regularly form its plural as fa'lala. This is the interpretation of the majority of exegetes from Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, Mujahid and others, and the simile would then follow the well-known imagery in Arabic speech.

It is also said: "qaswara" is singular and means the lion. This is transmitted from Abu Hurayra and Zayd ibn Aslam. Ibn 'Abbas said it is the lion in Abyssinian (al-Habashiyya), so the disagreement in Ibn 'Abbas's statement is merely verbal. And from him: he denied that qaswar is a name for the lion, perhaps meaning that it is not in the original Arabic language. Ibn al-Subki counted it among the words in the Qur'an that are not in the language of the Arabs, in verses in which he mentioned this. Ibn Sida said: "Al-qaswar is the lion, and al-qaswara likewise; they feminized it as they said usama." On this reading, it is an original simile for a state of turning away mixed with terror from what the thunderous verses of the Qur'an contain, so that two images are combined in this sentence.

The choice of the word "qaswara" here is because it is suitable for both similes, while also observing the rhyme (fasila).

Ibn 'Abbas said it is the lion in Abyssinian (al-Habashiyya), so the disagreement in Ibn 'Abbas's statement is merely verbal. And from him: he denied that qaswar is a name for the lion, perhaps meaning that it is not in the original Arabic language. Ibn al-Subki counted it among the words in the Qur'an that are not in the language of the Arabs, in verses in which he mentioned this. Ibn Sida said: "Al-qaswar is the lion, and al-qaswara likewise; they feminized it as they said usama." On this reading, it is an original simile for a state of turning away mixed with terror from what the thunderous verses of the Qur'an contain, so that two images are combined in this sentence.

The choice of the word "qaswara" here is because it is suitable for both similes, while also observing the rhyme (fasila).

Verse 52: "Nay, every man among them desires that he be given scrolls spread open."

Page 331

This is a transitional digression (idrab intiqali) introducing another aspect of their obstinacy, since "Abu Jahl, 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayya, and others among the disbelievers of Quraysh said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'We will not believe you until a book comes to each one of us from Allah addressed to so-and-so son of so-and-so.'" This is among the varied forms of their denial that the Qur'an is sent down from Allah.

The word (suhuf, scrolls) is in the plural either because they demanded that every command or prohibition addressed to an individual come to him in its own scroll, or because, when they demanded that each of them be sent a scroll bearing his name, and they were a group acting in unison, the plural was used for this purpose; it is as if all the scrolls had come to each man among them.

Al-munashshara (spread open) means the opened, readable one, i.e., "we will not be satisfied with a folded scroll whose contents we do not know." It is an intensive form (mubalagha) of manshura. This intensification follows what the bare verb nashara implies: that the book is open and clear, of the familiar kind of scrolls. In the hadith about stoning: "they spread out the Torah" (fa-nasharu al-Tawrah).

Kallā (nay, not so) is a rejection of the apparent meaning of their words and of what they intended by them, and a deterrent from that: that is, it cannot be that they have that.

Then He turns away from their words with another refutation, using the particle of turning away (bal, "rather"), and says: "Rather, they do not fear the Hereafter." That is, what they said was nothing but an evasion. Had a Book been sent down to them, they would not have believed while they feared the Hereafter; that is, they do not believe in it. He has used the expression "not fearing the Hereafter" as a metonymy (kināya) for "not believing in the Hereafter," because if they believed in it they would have feared it, since the normal course is that one fears its punishment. And the denial of the Hereafter altogether is their making the Hereafter-life impossible, as a consequence of their denial of the Qur'an.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 74, verses 54–55:

﴿Nay, indeed it is a reminder.﴾ ﴿So whoever wills may remember it.﴾ ﴿And you will not remember except that Allah wills.﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 54–56] (

[Page 332]
(*Kalla*) is a second prohibition, emphasizing the first one before it. That is, they will not be given scrolls unrolled, nor will they be singled out for [special revelation] except through the Qur'an.

The sentence (﴿Indeed, it is a reminder﴾) gives the reason for the prohibition against their request that scrolls be unrolled upon them: this Qur'an is a great reminder. This is like His saying, exalted is He (﴿They say, "Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say, "Signs are only with Allah, and I am only a clear warner."﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 50] ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book, recited to them? Indeed in that is mercy and a reminder for a people who believe.﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 51]). The pronoun in (*innahu*) refers to the Qur'an, which is known from the context, and similar instances are numerous in the Qur'an. The indefinite form *tadhkira* (reminder) is for magnification.

His saying (﴿So whoever wills may remember it﴾) is a consequence drawn from the fact that it is a reminder. Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He, in surah al-Muzzammil (﴿Indeed, this is a reminder, so whoever wills may take to his Lord a way.﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 19]).

This is an indirect encouragement to remember: remembering is subject to your will, so if you will, then remember.

The apparent pronoun in *dhakarahu* may refer to what the pronoun in (*innahu*) refers to, namely the Qur'an, in which case it is an elision and connection, its original form being *dhakara bihi* (he remembered by it).

It may also refer to Allah, exalted is He, even though no mention of His name has preceded in these verses, because it is present in the context, in the manner of His saying (﴿Indeed, this is a reminder, so whoever wills may take to his Lord a way﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 19]).

The pronoun in "*shaa*" (wills) refers to (*man*, whoever), meaning: whoever wishes to remember, remembers by means of the Qur'an. This is like His saying earlier (﴿for whoever of you wills to go forward or to remain behind﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 37]) and His saying in surah al-Muzzammil (﴿so whoever wills may take to his Lord a way﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 19]).

This is a warning to people that remembrance through the Qur'an occurs when they will to remember through it. Willing requires reflection on what saves them from being held accountable for negligence, and they have no excuse for neglecting it, as has already been discussed in surah al-Muzzammil.

The sentence (﴿And you will not remember except that Allah wills﴾) is a parenthetical clause at the end of the speech, serving to inform them of this reality, and the *waw* is parenthetical.

The meaning is: the remembrance of those whom they wish to remember only occurs when conditioned by Allah's will that they remember. This has been repeated in the Qur'an so often that it alerts us that it is a established reality, like His saying (﴿And you will not will except that Allah wills﴾). Here He says (﴿Nay, indeed it is a reminder﴾ [‘Abasa: 11] ﴿so whoever wills may remember it﴾ [‘Abasa: 12]). From this we know that people have a will which is the basis of the legal obligations of the Sharia and of reward and punishment in this world and the Hereafter. Among the scholars of verification (*ahl al-tahqiq*) among the theologians, it is expressed as *kasb* (acquisition), as verified by al-Ash'ari, and among the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school) as *al-qudra al-haditha* (created power). These are two closely related expressions. And Allah, exalted is He, has the supreme will, which no obstacle can prevent and no compeller can force. So when its attachment is not directed toward the willing of one of His servants, nothing of that servant's desire is realized.

This will is what is expressed as *tawfiq* (divine enablement) when it is attached to empowering the servant with the motive toward obedience and the carrying out of the divine commands, and as *khidhlan* (divine abandonment) when it is attached to leaving him in the error into which his misguided opinions and corrupt, destructive desires have plunged him, turning him away from the laws of Allah and the call of His messengers. And when it is attached to lifting the servant out of the states of misguidance and to illuminating the path of good for his insight, it is called *lutf* (divine kindness), as with its attachment to the faith and righteousness of ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab after he had been in obstinacy. This is the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He (﴿Whomever Allah wills to guide, He expands his breast to Islam; and whomever He wills to leave astray, He makes his breast tight and constricted, as if he were climbing into the sky﴾ [al-An'am: 125]).

This is the outcome that results from combining the textual evidences of the Sharia, which indicate that the matter belongs to Allah, with the evidences that establish accountability for misguidance. Its greatest interpretation is in His saying, exalted is He (﴿If good befalls them, they say, "This is from Allah"; and if evil befalls them, they say, "This is from you." Say, "All is from Allah." So what is wrong with these people that they can hardly understand any statement?﴾ [al-Nisa': 78] ﴿Whatever good reaches you is from Allah, and whatever evil reaches you is from yourself﴾ [al-Nisa': 79]). Allah has a secret in His creation, which He placed between them and His essence as a veil, and He signaled toward it through the promise and the threat, as reward and punishment.

Nafi' and Ya'qub read (*wa-ma tadhkurun*) with a *ta'* (second person), as an *iltifat* (shift of grammatical person), whereas the majority read it with a *ya'* (third person), as absence. The meaning is: it is characteristic of them to persist in not being reminded by this reminder, unless Allah wills to grant them enablement and to show them kindness, so that He creates a transformation in the disposition of whomever He wills to enable and to show kindness to. Allah has indeed willed this concerning those who believed before the revelation of this verse and those who believed after its revelation.
